title: The general half-integral TSP frontier
subfield: Routing, network optimization, and mathematical foundations
open: Is there a \(4/3\)-approximation algorithm for metric TSP on every instance whose subtour LP optimum is half-integral, extending beyond the structural subclasses currently tractable?
status: A 2025 result achieves \(4/3\) for half-integral cycle-cut instances; the unrestricted half-integral case is broader. Jin, Klein, and Williamson (2025), *A 4/3-approximation algorithm for half-integral cycle cut instances of the TSP*, DOI:10.1007/s10107-025-02193-5.
solved_when: A \(4/3\)-approximation is proven (or given) for all metric TSP instances with an optimal half-integral subtour solution, not restricted to cycle-cut or other structural subclasses.
why: It could isolate the combinatorial obstruction behind the general TSP conjecture.
key_works: Jin, Klein, and Williamson (2025), *A 4/3-approximation algorithm for half-integral cycle cut instances of the TSP*, DOI:10.1007/s10107-025-02193-5.

title: Coupled traffic–charging–electricity equilibrium
subfield: Routing, network optimization, and mathematical foundations
open: When route choice, finite charging queues, battery feasibility, and distribution-grid constraints all jointly shape feasible travel, can we prove that an equilibrium exists and compute it? More precisely, identify the conditions under which a coupled traffic–charging–electricity equilibrium exists and construct provably convergent algorithms for finding it.
status: Dynamic energy-feasible traffic equilibria are established in restricted models (Graf, Harks, and Palkar, 2022, *Dynamic Traffic Assignment for Electric Vehicles*, arXiv:2207.04454); endogenous charging-power and queue feedback introduce additional coupling that these results do not cover.
solved_when: Existence conditions are established for the fully coupled model — where charging power and queues are endogenous and distribution-grid constraints bind — together with an algorithm proven to converge to such an equilibrium.
why: Without a joint theory, traffic models and electricity models can each assume behavior of the other that is mutually incompatible, yielding plans that fail when implemented together.
key_works: Graf, Harks, and Palkar (2022), *Dynamic Traffic Assignment for Electric Vehicles*, arXiv:2207.04454.

title: Transferable urban macroscopic fundamental diagrams
open: Under what observable conditions does an aggregate flow–accumulation relationship for an urban network hold across days, neighborhoods, and interventions? Formally, this asks for measurable properties of the network and its congestion distribution that guarantee a macroscopic fundamental diagram transfers without complete recalibration.
status: Urban-scale macroscopic relationships have been measured since 2008 (Geroliminis and Daganzo, 2008, *Existence of urban-scale macroscopic fundamental diagrams: Some experimental findings*); their portability is known to depend on network structure and congestion distribution, as examined empirically by Wang et al. (2015), *An Empirical Analysis of Macroscopic Fundamental Diagrams for Sendai Road Networks*.
solved_when: A characterization is given of the observable conditions (in terms of network structure and congestion distribution) under which an urban flow–accumulation relationship transfers across days, neighborhoods, and interventions without recalibration, supported by theory or empirical validation.
why: A solution enables citywide traffic control using far fewer state variables, since a single transferable aggregate relation replaces network-level calibration.
key_works: Geroliminis and Daganzo (2008), *Existence of urban-scale macroscopic fundamental diagrams: Some experimental findings*; Wang et al. (2015), *An Empirical Analysis of Macroscopic Fundamental Diagrams for Sendai Road Networks*.

title: Causal interpretation of network hysteresis
open: Can we disentangle the contributions of spatial congestion patterns, route changes, measurement aggregation, and demand history to the hysteresis observed in network flow–accumulation diagrams? In formal terms, this asks for a causal decomposition of the loop phenomenon that identifies which mechanism produces which part of the observed hysteresis.
status: Hysteresis is observed and modeled, but the same aggregate loop can conceal different internal states, so the causal separation remains unresolved. Key work: Wang, Wada, Akamatsu, and Hara (2015), *An Empirical Analysis of Macroscopic Fundamental Diagrams for Sendai Road Networks*.
solved_when: A method or framework exists that separately attributes the observed hysteresis in a network flow–accumulation diagram to spatial congestion patterns, route changes, measurement aggregation, and demand history, and demonstrates that the attribution is causal rather than merely descriptive.
why: It determines whether a controller can safely act on accumulation alone: if identical aggregate loops can conceal different internal states, acting on the aggregate alone risks misinformed control decisions.
key_works: Wang, Wada, Akamatsu, and Hara (2015), *An Empirical Analysis of Macroscopic Fundamental Diagrams for Sendai Road Networks*.

title: Long-run rebound from traffic smoothing
open: Does smoothing traffic — for example, with coordinated automated vehicles — still reduce total energy use and delay once travelers adapt by changing when they leave, which routes they take, where they go, and how often they travel? The question is to measure long-run systemwide outcomes rather than short-run flow improvements.
status: Large field demonstrations, such as the CIRCLES consortium's 100-AV field test (Ameli et al., 2024, arXiv:2404.15533), address immediate traffic dynamics, but long-run demand responses require different experimental designs; Duranton and Turner (2011), DOI:10.1257/aer.101.6.2616, exemplify the induced-travel concern.
solved_when: An experimental (or quasi-experimental) design capable of capturing long-run demand responses demonstrates a measured difference in total energy and delay after full traveler adjustment, relative to pre-smoothing conditions.
why: Short-run fuel savings from smoother flow need not persist as systemwide savings; travel-demand adaptation can erode or reverse them, as analogous rebound effects in energy economics suggest.
key_works: Ameli et al. (2024), *Designing, simulating, and performing the 100-AV field test for the CIRCLES consortium*, arXiv:2404.15533; Duranton and Turner (2011), DOI:10.1257/aer.101.6.2616.

title: Spillback-safe multimodal max-pressure control
open: Can a signal-control policy jointly handle finite road storage, pedestrian clearance times, transit priority, and time-varying turning fractions while still provably stabilizing the network? Formally, the question is whether a max-pressure-style controller can incorporate these multimodal constraints and retain a network-stability guarantee.
status: Capacity-aware backpressure (Gregoire et al., *Capacity-aware backpressure traffic signal control*, DOI:10.1109/TCNS.2014.2378871) addresses important finite-buffer limitations, but a combined multimodal stability guarantee remains an open and stronger target.
solved_when: A controller is designed that accounts for finite link storage (spillback), pedestrian clearance, and transit priority under changing turning fractions, with a proof that it stabilizes the traffic network under these conditions.
why: Optimizing vehicle throughput alone can starve pedestrians of crossing time or cause queues that block neighboring intersections; a combined guarantee prevents these failure modes.
key_works: Gregoire et al., *Capacity-aware backpressure traffic signal control*, DOI:10.1109/TCNS.2014.2378871.

title: Joint freeway–urban perimeter control
open: Can freeway access, urban boundary inflows, and internal signal timing be jointly controlled so that congestion is genuinely reduced rather than shifted elsewhere? Formally, is there a coordinated perimeter-and-freeway control scheme that remains stable under spillback and avoids relocating queues across network or jurisdictional boundaries?
status: Regional macroscopic control and freeway models exist — urban-scale macroscopic fundamental diagrams per Geroliminis and Daganzo (2008), *Existence of urban-scale macroscopic fundamental diagrams*, and freeway network MFDs per Cassidy et al. (2011), *Macroscopic Fundamental Diagrams for Freeway Networks*, DOI:10.3141/2260-02 — but their joint spillback-aware operation requires stronger coupled models and field evidence.
solved_when: A coupled freeway–urban control scheme is demonstrated (in model or field) that coordinates ramp/access control, perimeter inflows, and internal signals without producing net queue transfer to another network or jurisdiction, supported by coupled spillback-aware models and field evidence.
why: Freeway and arterial congestion cannot always be optimized independently, so local improvements can silently export their queues; a genuine joint scheme is required for real network-wide relief.
key_works: Geroliminis and Daganzo (2008), *Existence of urban-scale macroscopic fundamental diagrams*; Cassidy et al. (2011), *Macroscopic Fundamental Diagrams for Freeway Networks*, DOI:10.3141/2260-02.

title: Micromobility’s true displaced mode
open: What trip does a shared micromobility ride actually replace? We need empirical measurement of the counterfactual mode — whether each ride substitutes for walking, public transport, or a private car, or represents a trip that would not otherwise occur.
status: Lifecycle analyses (e.g., Hollingsworth, Copeland, and Johnson, 2019, on dockless e-scooters) show results are sensitive to use patterns and alternatives; observed substitution varies by place and user.
solved_when: A rigorous measurement exists of the counterfactual displaced mode across walking, public transport, private cars, and induced (otherwise non-occurring) trips, capturing how substitution varies by place and user.
why: It determines whether micromobility deployment actually reduces emissions and congestion, since lifecycle outcomes are highly sensitive to use patterns and the alternatives replaced.
key_works: Hollingsworth, Copeland, and Johnson (2019), *Are e-scooters polluters? The environmental impacts of shared dockless electric scooters*, DOI:10.1088/1748-9326/ab2da8.

title: Wheelchairs as certified aircraft seats
subfield: Accessibility, disability, and complete trip chains
open: Can a wheelchair, secured in an aircraft cabin, protect its occupant as well as a certified aircraft seat does in a crash? The goal is to demonstrate crashworthy wheelchair-and-restraint configurations across a representative range of chairs, occupants, and aircraft loading conditions.
status: A 2021 assessment by the National Academies (2021), *Technical Feasibility of a Wheelchair Securement Concept for Airline Travel: A Preliminary Assessment* (DOI:10.17226/26323), found the technical feasibility of a wheelchair securement concept worth pursuing; however, feasibility is not the same as universal certification, and no such certified configuration yet exists.
solved_when: Crashworthy wheelchair-and-restraint configurations have been demonstrated experimentally across a representative range of wheelchair types, occupant sizes, and aircraft loading conditions — going beyond a feasibility assessment to certification-grade evidence.
why: Success would eliminate the dangerous manual transfers between wheelchair and aircraft seat that injure travelers today, and end the damage to essential mobility equipment that currently occurs in transit.
key_works: National Academies (2021), *Technical Feasibility of a Wheelchair Securement Concept for Airline Travel: A Preliminary Assessment*, DOI:10.17226/26323.

title: Interoperable aircraft wheelchair securement
subfield: Accessibility, disability, and complete trip chains
open: Can a standardized securement interface be developed that safely accommodates diverse wheelchairs aboard aircraft, without each chair–aircraft combination becoming a bespoke installation?
status: Securement concepts exist, but compatibility, loading, and operational integration remain broader engineering requirements. Key work: National Academies (2021), *Technical Feasibility of a Wheelchair Securement Concept for Airline Travel*, DOI:10.17226/26323.
solved_when: A securement interface is demonstrated that safely accommodates diverse wheelchairs and integrates with aircraft loading and fleet operations, so that no chair–aircraft pairing requires a bespoke installation.
why: A technically safe niche configuration may still be unusable at fleet scale; interoperability is what makes securement practical across an airline fleet rather than in isolated demonstrations.
key_works: National Academies (2021), *Technical Feasibility of a Wheelchair Securement Concept for Airline Travel*, DOI:10.17226/26323.

title: Net flight benefit of boundary-layer ingestion
open: Does boundary-layer ingestion deliver a net energy benefit on a real aircraft mission once the penalties of distorted inflow, installation, structure, control, and off-design operation are all paid for? In other words, can the idealized propulsor-level savings survive an integrated flight demonstration?
status: Modeling and coupled optimization have advanced, but isolated propulsor results and idealized benefit estimates do not settle integrated flight performance. Key work: Hendricks et al. (2018), *A Review of Boundary Layer Ingestion Modeling Approaches for Use in Conceptual Design*, NASA NTRS 20180005165.
solved_when: An experimental or high-fidelity integrated demonstration shows net mission energy savings after accounting for distorted inflow, installation effects, structural changes, control, and off-design operation.
why: A validated benefit would recover energy otherwise lost in the aircraft wake, translating a long-claimed theoretical advantage into real mission fuel savings.
key_works: Hendricks et al. (2018), *A Review of Boundary Layer Ingestion Modeling Approaches for Use in Conceptual Design*, NASA NTRS 20180005165.

title: Closed-loop planning metrics aligned with safety
open: Which benchmark metrics actually predict safe and efficient closed-loop driving behavior, as opposed to merely measuring similarity to a recorded human trajectory? More formally, the problem is to identify or design evaluation metrics whose optimization corresponds to competent closed-loop performance rather than high similarity scores.
status: nuPlan supplies closed-loop evaluation; deciding which metrics are causally meaningful remains a further problem. Key reference: Caesar et al. (2021), *nuPlan: A closed-loop ML-based planning benchmark for autonomous vehicles*, arXiv:2106.11810.
solved_when: A set of metrics is shown to be causally meaningful for closed-loop safety and efficiency — that is, metrics that demonstrably predict (rather than merely correlate with open-loop trajectory similarity) safe, efficient closed-loop driving behavior on closed-loop evaluation.
why: A plausible trajectory prediction is not necessarily a competent driving policy; without validated metrics, benchmark scores can certify imitation rather than safe operation.
key_works: Caesar et al. (2021), *nuPlan: A closed-loop ML-based planning benchmark for autonomous vehicles*, arXiv:2106.11810.

title: Metric TSP subtour-relaxation gap
subfield: Routing, network optimization, and mathematical foundations
open: Is the integrality gap of the subtour-elimination linear programming relaxation for the symmetric metric traveling salesman problem exactly \(4/3\)? Formally, prove or disprove that the supremum over all instances of the ratio between the optimal tour length and the subtour-LP optimum equals \(4/3\).
status: The problem is decades old. Exact computations reported in 2026 by Cook, Hougardy, and Petrich (2026), *Extending Exact Integrality Gap Computations for the Metric TSP*, arXiv:2603.12995, extend verification through 15 vertices, but finite verification does not settle arbitrary instances.
solved_when: A proof (or refutation) of the exact value \(4/3\) for the integrality gap on arbitrary metric instances — finite verification through any number of vertices does not suffice.
why: It would sharpen a foundational lower bound used throughout routing optimization, fixing the precise worst-case quality guarantee of the central LP relaxation in TSP approximation.
key_works: Cook, Hougardy, and Petrich (2026), *Extending Exact Integrality Gap Computations for the Metric TSP*, arXiv:2603.12995.

title: A general \(4/3\)-approximation for metric TSP
subfield: Routing, network optimization, and mathematical foundations
open: Is there a polynomial-time algorithm that, on every symmetric metric instance of the traveling salesperson problem, returns a tour of cost at most \(4/3\) times the optimum? Formally, construct such an algorithm matching the conjectured \(4/3\) approximation guarantee.
status: A better-than-\(3/2\) approximation is established, but it does not approach the conjectured \(4/3\) guarantee. Key works: Karlin, Klein, and Oveis Gharan (2023), *A deterministic better-than-3/2 approximation algorithm for metric TSP*, DOI:10.1007/978-3-031-32726-1_19; Cook et al. (2026), arXiv:2603.12995.
solved_when: A polynomial-time algorithm is given with a proven worst-case approximation ratio of at most \(4/3\) for all symmetric metric TSP instances.
why: It would tighten worst-case guarantees for distribution, inspection, and service routing, where tours produced in practice are still bounded by looser theoretical ratios.
key_works: Karlin, Klein, and Oveis Gharan (2023), *A deterministic better-than-3/2 approximation algorithm for metric TSP*, DOI:10.1007/978-3-031-32726-1_19; Cook et al. (2026), arXiv:2603.12995.

title: Variance of random Euclidean tour length
subfield: Routing, network optimization, and mathematical foundations
open: How variable is the length of the shortest tour through points sampled uniformly at random in a disc? More precisely, what is the variance of the optimal tour length, both at finite sample sizes and in the asymptotic regime?
status: The leading tour-length scaling is classical, following Beardwood, Halton, and Hammersley (1959), *The shortest path through many points*; the variance question itself was explicitly posed at Dagstuhl in 2024, and is also discussed by Connors, in Correa et al. (2025), *Dynamic Traffic Models in Transportation Science*, §4.2.
solved_when: An expression (exact or asymptotic) for the finite-size and asymptotic variance of the optimal tour length through uniformly sampled points in a disc is established.
why: It would quantify the uncertainty in spatial logistics approximations that rely on expected tour-length scalings.
key_works: Beardwood, Halton, and Hammersley (1959), *The shortest path through many points*; Connors, in Correa et al. (2025), *Dynamic Traffic Models in Transportation Science*, §4.2.

title: A three-approximation for unsplittable capacitated routing
subfield: Routing, network optimization, and mathematical foundations
open: Is there a polynomial-time 3-approximation for the unsplittable capacitated vehicle routing problem on general metrics? Formally, find such an algorithm, or establish a stronger approximation barrier showing that ratio 3 cannot be achieved in polynomial time.
status: Zhao and Xiao (2026), *Improved Approximations for the Unsplittable Capacitated Vehicle Routing Problem*, arXiv:2601.21660, report ratios below 3.1759 for variable capacity and below 3.0897 for fixed capacity.
solved_when: A polynomial-time algorithm achieving approximation ratio 3 for general metric unsplittable capacitated vehicle routing is given, or a hardness result is proved that rules out a polynomial-time 3-approximation.
why: It addresses indivisible deliveries whose demands cannot be divided among vehicles, closing the gap between current ratios and the natural barrier of 3.
key_works: Zhao and Xiao (2026), *Improved Approximations for the Unsplittable Capacitated Vehicle Routing Problem*, arXiv:2601.21660.

title: Tight approximation for capacitated arc routing
subfield: Routing, network optimization, and mathematical foundations
open: Close the approximation gap for undirected unit-demand capacitated arc routing: can a uniform 2-approximation be achieved, and can matching lower bounds establish its tightness?
status: A 2025 algorithm by Zhao and Xiao improves the longstanding bound to \(5/2-\Theta(1/\sqrt{k})\), where \(k\) is the vehicle capacity, in *An Improved Approximation Algorithm for the Capacitated Arc Routing Problem*, arXiv:2508.05471.
solved_when: A polynomial-time algorithm achieves approximation ratio 2 uniformly (independent of vehicle capacity k), or a matching hardness result shows this is impossible.
why: Tight guarantees directly affect how municipalities plan waste collection, street inspection, sweeping, and winter maintenance, where even small ratio improvements yield large operational savings.
key_works: Zhao and Xiao (2025), *An Improved Approximation Algorithm for the Capacitated Arc Routing Problem*, arXiv:2508.05471.

title: Railway Convoy Conjecture
subfield: Routing, network optimization, and mathematical foundations
open: In a directed acyclic railway network where trains share a common origin, destination, and travel times, and a minimum entry headway is imposed, must an optimal makespan solution always use train paths that are either identical or pairwise disjoint? Formally, prove that no optimal solution requires paths that partially overlap.
status: The conjecture is established for three trains and is explicitly open for four or more trains. The problem appears in Eickenberg, in Correa et al. (2025), *Dynamic Traffic Models in Transportation Science*, §4.3.
solved_when: The conjecture is proven for any number of trains in the directed acyclic model with common origin, destination, travel times, and minimum entry headway; equivalently, a counterexample is exhibited for four or more trains.
why: A proof would establish that optimal schedules never require intermediate waiting, simplifying the structure of optimal convoy solutions and potentially the algorithms that find them.
key_works: Eickhoff, in Correa et al. (2025), *Dynamic Traffic Models in Transportation Science*, §4.3.

title: String stability with changing vehicle order
open: Can a vehicle platoon remain string stable — bounded disturbance amplification — when heterogeneous vehicles repeatedly join, leave, and cut in, subject to actuator limits and uncertain human responses? Formally, is there a control design guaranteeing string stability under such switching platoon compositions and uncertainties?
status: Strong safety and stability results exist under specified dynamics — e.g., Berger et al. (2026), *String stability and guaranteed safety via funnel cruise control* — but arbitrary switching of platoon composition and real cut-in behavior exceed the assumptions of many of these results.
solved_when: A control scheme is exhibited that provably guarantees bounded disturbance amplification for heterogeneous platoons under repeated joining, leaving, and cut-in events, with actuator limits and uncertain human driver responses modeled.
why: Without it, local cruise-control improvements can amplify braking disturbances downstream and propagate collisions through the platoon; with it, adaptive cruise controllers remain safe under realistic traffic mixing.
key_works: Berger et al. (2026), *String stability and guaranteed safety via funnel cruise control*.

title: Multiple-depot capacitated routing below four
subfield: Routing, network optimization, and mathematical foundations
open: What is the tight approximation threshold for metric multiple-depot, unit-demand capacitated routing? A concrete next target is a 3-approximation, improving on the current best ratio.
status: Friggstad and Mömke (2025) obtain a 3.9365-approximation in *Approximating Multiple-Depot Capacitated Vehicle Routing via LP Rounding*, arXiv:2510.05321.
solved_when: An approximation algorithm matching the tight threshold is given; in particular, a factor-3 approximation would meet the stated target.
why: Joint depot assignment and routing remain harder than solving independent depot territories, so progress here clarifies the true cost of coupling depots in capacitated routing.
key_works: Friggstad and Mömke (2025), *Approximating Multiple-Depot Capacitated Vehicle Routing via LP Rounding*, arXiv:2510.05321.

title: Dynamic routing games with heterogeneous deadlines
subfield: Routing, network optimization, and mathematical foundations
open: Do equilibria exist, and how inefficient can they be, when travelers in a dynamic routing game each face their own deadline and lateness penalty rather than a common objective? A complete answer would characterize equilibrium existence and quantify the price of anarchy for such heterogeneous-deadline flows over time.
status: Deadline-based bicriteria models have partial theory, and heterogeneous deadlines remain an explicitly identified extension (Oosterwijk, Schmand, and Schröder (2024), *Bicriteria Nash Flows over Time*, DOI:10.1016/j.geb.2024.06.002; Dagstuhl 24281, §4.1).
solved_when: Equilibrium existence and inefficiency are characterized for dynamic routing games with heterogeneous deadlines and lateness penalties (e.g., a price-of-anarchy bound and existence conditions).
why: It models deliveries and appointments far more realistically than travel-time-only objectives, connecting routing games to real scheduling constraints.
key_works: Oosterwijk, Schmand, and Schröder (2024), *Bicriteria Nash Flows over Time*, DOI:10.1016/j.geb.2024.06.002; Dagstuhl 24281, §4.1.

title: Causal mechanism of capacity drop
open: Can field experiments be designed that distinguish which of the competing explanations actually causes the reduction in discharge flow once congestion sets in, rather than merely fitting the same aggregate curve?
status: Existing models reproduce capacity drop, but matching observations does not uniquely identify the responsible behavioral mechanism. Key work: Treiber, Kesting, and Helbing (2006), *Understanding widely scattered traffic flows, the capacity drop, platoons, and times-to-collision as effects of variance-driven time gaps*, DOI:10.1103/PhysRevE.74.016123.
solved_when: A field experiment (or experimental design) is produced whose observable outcomes discriminate between the competing mechanism hypotheses for discharge-flow reduction, going beyond reproducing the aggregate capacity-drop curve.
why: Different causal mechanisms imply different effective control strategies, so identifying the true mechanism determines which interventions will actually work.
key_works: Treiber, Kesting, and Helbing (2006), *Understanding widely scattered traffic flows, the capacity drop, platoons, and times-to-collision as effects of variance-driven time gaps*, DOI:10.1103/PhysRevE.74.016123.

title: Predictive distribution of traffic breakdown
open: Can we forecast traffic breakdown before it happens — assigning calibrated probabilities to when and where congestion will onset, conditioned on demand, vehicle composition, weather, and recent disturbances?
status: Stochastic and behavioral models explain the variability of scattered traffic flows, but transferable, intervention-sensitive breakdown probabilities remain a forecasting target. Key work: Treiber, Kesting, and Helbing (2006), *Understanding widely scattered traffic flows…*, DOI:10.1103/PhysRevE.74.016123.
solved_when: A predictive model delivers calibrated breakdown probabilities (in time and location) that transfer across sites and respond correctly to interventions, validated against observed congestion onsets.
why: Calibrated forecasts enable preventive control actions — ramp metering, speed limits, routing — taken before queues form, rather than reactive management after breakdown.
key_works: Treiber, Kesting, and Helbing (2006), *Understanding widely scattered traffic flows…*, DOI:10.1103/PhysRevE.74.016123.

title: Adaptive congestion-region partitioning
open: Can a city be partitioned into congestion regions whose aggregate traffic dynamics stay identifiable even as congestion boundaries move, while the partitioning itself remains stable and does not oscillate? More formally, the question asks for a partition scheme with predictive validity of the regional dynamics and closed-loop guarantees under changing partitions.
status: Dynamic clustering methods exist, but predictive validity and closed-loop guarantees under changing partitions remain separate, unmet requirements. Key work: Saeedmanesh and Geroliminis (2017), *Dynamic clustering and propagation of congestion in heterogeneously congested urban traffic networks*.
solved_when: A partitioning method is given whose resulting regions retain identifiable aggregate traffic dynamics as congestion boundaries shift, and for which repartitioning is provably stable — that is, the partitions do not fluctuate unstably in response to the dynamics they describe.
why: Fixed administrative zones often poorly represent moving queues, so region-level models built on them degrade; an adaptive partition would let aggregate traffic models track congestion as it actually propagates.
key_works: Saeedmanesh and Geroliminis (2017), *Dynamic clustering and propagation of congestion in heterogeneously congested urban traffic networks*.

title: Computable spillback equilibria at metropolitan scale
open: Can we compute dynamic traffic equilibria at metropolitan scale when links have finite storage, spillback, and realistic junction interactions — and certify how far the computed solution is from true equilibrium? Formally, the goal is scalable algorithms for spillback equilibria whose output carries a certified residual bound.
status: Equilibrium existence with spillback is not wholly open; the distinct remaining gaps are computational scalability and stronger operational models. Key work: Sering and Vargas Koch (2018), *Nash Flows over Time with Spillback and Kinematic Waves*, arXiv:1807.05862.
solved_when: An algorithm computes dynamic equilibria for networks with finite storage, spillback, and realistic junction interactions at metropolitan (scalable) size, with a certified residual guarantee on the solution.
why: Point-queue approximations can miss gridlock and upstream blocking, so assignment results built on them can mispredict large-scale network behavior under congestion.
key_works: Sering and Vargas Koch (2018), *Nash Flows over Time with Spillback and Kinematic Waves*, arXiv:1807.05862.

title: Day-to-day learning without unstable route oscillation
open: Can day-to-day traveler learning converge to a stable traffic assignment when the information travelers receive is delayed, incomplete, and shared strategically? More precisely, the task is to find empirically defensible learning rules that provably converge, or else to characterize the persistent oscillations they produce.
status: Bounded-rationality and information-sharing models have been simulated; convergence and behavioral identification remain model-dependent. Key work: Yu, Han, and Ochieng (2018), *Day-to-Day Dynamic Traffic Assignment with Imperfect Information, Bounded Rationality and Information Sharing*, arXiv:1811.10729.
solved_when: Either an empirically defensible traveler-learning rule under delayed, incomplete, strategically shared information is shown to converge, or the resulting persistent oscillations are formally characterized.
why: Navigation systems can create synchronized rerouting rather than equilibrium, so understanding when learning stabilizes or oscillates matters for real network performance.
key_works: Yu, Han, and Ochieng (2018), *Day-to-Day Dynamic Traffic Assignment with Imperfect Information, Bounded Rationality and Information Sharing*, arXiv:1811.10729.

title: Driver-model parameters under intervention
open: Which car-following and route-learning parameters, once fitted to observational data, remain invariant when a pricing scheme, automation, road redesign, or information provision changes the traffic system? Formally: identify the subset of driver-model parameters that is causal-invariant, and hence transportable, across such interventions.
status: The state of the art is observational calibration, but successful observational calibration does not establish that fitted parameters survive interventions. Key works: Yu, Han, and Ochieng (2018), *Day-to-Day Dynamic Traffic Assignment…*; Treiber et al. (2006), DOI:10.1103/PhysRevE.74.016123. Related threads: causal invariance; structural-model transportability.
solved_when: A principled identification test (experimental or data-driven) determines which fitted car-following and route-learning parameters survive pricing, automation, road redesign, and information interventions — showing which are invariant and which must be re-estimated.
why: Policy simulations fail when driver behavior changes precisely because a policy is introduced; invariance knowledge tells modelers which parameters can be carried over and which invalidate forecasts.
key_works: Yu, Han, and Ochieng (2018), *Day-to-Day Dynamic Traffic Assignment…*; Treiber et al. (2006), DOI:10.1103/PhysRevE.74.016123.

title: Minimum effective penetration of traffic-smoothing vehicles
open: What is the smallest fraction of controllable vehicles that reliably suppresses traffic disturbances, and how does this threshold depend on road geometry, demand regimes, and human-driver populations?
status: In ring-road field experiments, a single controlled vehicle damped stop-and-go waves (Stern et al. (2018), *Dissipation of stop-and-go waves via control of autonomous vehicles: Field experiments*, DOI:10.1016/j.trc.2018.02.005), but this is not a universal penetration threshold.
solved_when: A quantitative penetration threshold is established that holds reliably across the specified road geometries, demand regimes, and human-driver populations, rather than for a single experimental configuration.
why: It sets realistic deployment requirements for partial automation, telling operators how many controlled vehicles are actually needed for smoothing to work.
key_works: Stern et al. (2018), *Dissipation of stop-and-go waves via control of autonomous vehicles: Field experiments*, DOI:10.1016/j.trc.2018.02.005.

title: Replicable open-road smoothing benefits
open: Can the fuel-economy, safety, and throughput effects produced by a small fraction of controlled vehicles be reproduced on independent freeway sites? A formal statement: replicate controlled-vehicle smoothing effects across geographically and operationally distinct freeways using preregistered energy, safety, and throughput endpoints.
status: CIRCLES implemented a 100-vehicle field experiment, documented in Ameli et al. (2024), *Designing, simulating, and performing the 100-AV field test for the CIRCLES consortium*, arXiv:2404.15533; broader geographic and operational replication remains a separate, unmet evidence requirement.
solved_when: Controlled-vehicle effects are replicated in independent field experiments at freeway sites beyond the original, with energy, safety, and throughput endpoints specified by preregistration before data collection.
why: It separates genuinely deployable benefits from site-specific demonstration effects, determining whether controlled smoothing generalizes to real traffic networks.
key_works: Ameli et al. (2024), *Designing, simulating, and performing the 100-AV field test for the CIRCLES consortium*, arXiv:2404.15533.

title: Safe platooning through communication outages
open: Can a vehicular platoon remain provably collision-free and string-stable even when inter-vehicle communication degrades? In particular, we seek controllers that maintain safety and acceptable disturbance amplification under burst packet loss, delayed messages, and transitions between cooperative and independent operating modes.
status: Guaranteed controllers exist for specified sensing and dynamics, as in Berger et al. (2026), *String stability and guaranteed safety via funnel cruise control*, but realistic communication faults still require integrated certification; related work addresses fault-tolerant distributed control and networked control under adversarial delay.
solved_when: A controller design is given, together with a certification argument, that guarantees collision avoidance and acceptable string-stability (disturbance amplification bounds) under the specified communication faults: burst packet loss, message delays, and mode transitions between cooperative and independent control.
why: Communication failure in a platoon must not trigger coordinated unsafe braking, so the safety guarantee has to survive the very faults the communication layer introduces.
key_works: Berger et al. (2026), *String stability and guaranteed safety via funnel cruise control*.

title: Traffic control with unobservable queues
open: Can the true queue state at an intersection be inferred from sparse and biased connected-vehicle or crowdsourced data, with the resulting uncertainty explicitly propagated into signal control decisions?
status: Delay-based crowdsourced control has been demonstrated (Dixit et al. (2020), *A simple crowdsourced delay-based traffic signal control*), but missing users and changing sampling rates remain important observability problems; a connection exists to state estimation under missing-not-at-random observations.
solved_when: A method recovers actionable queue states from such partial observations and demonstrably accounts for missing users and changing sampling rates, feeding signal decisions that reflect the propagated uncertainty.
why: Most intersections cannot assume complete, reliable vehicle detection, so signal control must work from whatever biased samples are actually available.
key_works: Dixit et al. (2020), *A simple crowdsourced delay-based traffic signal control*.

title: Safe transfer of learned signal controllers
open: Can a signal controller trained with reinforcement learning be transferred to a new road network while guaranteeing that exploratory actions never violate safety constraints or destabilize traffic queues? Formally, the question is whether safe transfer across network and demand changes is achievable without fresh unsafe exploration in the target setting.
status: A 2026 study demonstrates parameter-sharing transfer to larger corridor networks, while arbitrary network and demand shifts remain broader targets. Key work: Song, Eder, Lawry, and Wilson (2026), *Systematic Analyses of Reinforcement Learning Controllers in Signalized Urban Corridors*, arXiv:2604.02025.
solved_when: A learned controller deployed on a new network maintains safety constraints and queue stability throughout adaptation, including under network and demand shifts beyond the larger corridor settings already demonstrated.
why: Without such transfer, every city must retrain controllers from scratch, which blocks practical deployment of learned traffic control.
key_works: Song, Eder, Lawry, and Wilson (2026), *Systematic Analyses of Reinforcement Learning Controllers in Signalized Urban Corridors*, arXiv:2604.02025.

title: Certified capacity regions for learned traffic control
open: Can we compute certified inner and outer bounds on the set of demand vectors that a learned traffic signal controller can stabilize, instead of judging it by average delay on a handful of chosen scenarios? Formally, the goal is a defensible capacity-region characterization for such controllers that holds beyond any particular test scenario.
status: Capacity-region evaluation has been developed for corridor experiments, notably in Song et al. (2026), *Systematic Analyses of Reinforcement Learning Controllers in Signalized Urban Corridors*, arXiv:2604.02025; certification for large uncertain networks remains a target.
solved_when: Defensible inner and outer bounds on the stabilizable demand region are computed for a learned controller, with certification extending to large uncertain networks rather than single corridors or selected scenarios.
why: Average performance hides catastrophic overload regions; certified bounds expose them before a learned controller is deployed.
key_works: Song et al. (2026), *Systematic Analyses of Reinforcement Learning Controllers in Signalized Urban Corridors*, arXiv:2604.02025.

title: Conditions for emergent green waves
open: When do decentralized traffic-signal controllers spontaneously produce persistent green-wave progression bands along a corridor, and when does purely local optimization instead destabilize coordination? More precisely, what conditions on the controllers and the network guarantee that emergent synchronization persists rather than degenerating?
status: Initial 2026 results suggest spontaneous green waves arise under parameter sharing, but general conditions are not established by those experiments; see Song et al. (2026), *Systematic Analyses of Reinforcement Learning Controllers in Signalized Urban Corridors*, arXiv:2604.02025.
solved_when: A characterization is given — analytic or experimentally validated — of the conditions under which decentralized controllers yield persistent green waves, and of when local optimization creates unstable coordination; the 2026 parameter-sharing findings must be either generalized or shown to be special cases.
why: It would let signal corridors achieve green-wave coordination without expensive centralized optimization, and would delimit the failure modes that make purely local control unreliable.
key_works: Song et al. (2026), *Systematic Analyses of Reinforcement Learning Controllers in Signalized Urban Corridors*, arXiv:2604.02025.

title: Auditable priority among conflicting road users
open: When an emergency vehicle, a bus, a pedestrian crossing, and ordinary traffic all claim priority at the same intersection, who yields — and by how much? Design real-time priority rules for these conflicting road users that come with explicit, auditable bounds on the delay and risk imposed on each group.
status: Individual priority mechanisms exist, but jointly auditable guarantees across groups remain a proposed system-level target. Key works include Gregoire et al., *Capacity-aware backpressure traffic signal control*, and Guihaire and Hao (2008), *Transit network design and scheduling: A global review*.
solved_when: A working priority mechanism exists that, in real time, assigns right-of-way among emergency vehicles, buses, pedestrians, and ordinary traffic while provably bounding the delay and risk imposed on each group.
why: Without joint guarantees, "priority" becomes ambiguous whenever several justified priorities conflict, and no party can be held accountable for who was made to wait or take on risk.
key_works: Gregoire et al., *Capacity-aware backpressure traffic signal control*; Guihaire and Hao (2008), *Transit network design and scheduling: A global review*.

title: Context-dependent induced-demand elasticities
subfield: Travel behavior, land use, and transport economics
open: How does induced travel demand vary with the context in which a road is built — initial congestion, land supply, road type, pricing, and development restrictions? More formally, can we characterize how the induced-travel elasticity depends on these setting-level variables, rather than assuming a single elasticity transfers across contexts?
status: Induced demand is established in the literature, and it is known that a single estimated elasticity does not automatically transfer between settings; Duranton and Turner (2011), *The Fundamental Law of Road Congestion: Evidence from US Cities*, DOI:10.1257/aer.101.6.2616.
solved_when: A quantified account of how induced travel (its elasticity) varies with initial congestion, land supply, road type, pricing, and development restrictions is available, showing where a single estimated elasticity fails to transfer between settings.
why: It improves forecasts of the congestion and emissions consequences of road expansion, which currently rest on elasticities that may not apply to the setting being forecast.
key_works: Duranton and Turner (2011), *The Fundamental Law of Road Congestion: Evidence from US Cities*, DOI:10.1257/aer.101.6.2616.

title: Welfare from capacity expansion beyond travel-time savings
subfield: Travel behavior, land use, and transport economics
open: Does expanding road capacity raise overall social welfare once all general-equilibrium responses are accounted for — new economic activity, household and firm relocation, freight productivity, pollution, and the distribution of gains and losses — or do these effects largely offset conventional travel-time benefits?
status: The current evidence establishes that traffic expands with roads — Duranton and Turner (2011), *The Fundamental Law of Road Congestion*, DOI:10.1257/aer.101.6.2616 — but this finding does not itself determine whether a particular project increases welfare.
solved_when: A method (theoretical or empirical) exists that estimates the general-equilibrium welfare effect of a specific road expansion project, capturing induced travel, new activities, relocation, freight productivity, pollution, and distributional incidence, and yields a sign and magnitude that can be compared against travel-time-savings-only estimates.
why: Without it, appraisals equate either congestion relief or induced traffic with the full social outcome, either overstating benefits by ignoring pollution and distributional costs or understating them by ignoring new activity and freight productivity gains.
key_works: Duranton and Turner (2011), *The Fundamental Law of Road Congestion*, DOI:10.1257/aer.101.6.2616.

title: Telework’s household-wide travel rebound
subfield: Travel behavior, land use, and transport economics
open: Does telework actually reduce a household's total travel and emissions once all its knock-on effects are counted? The question is how residential relocation, new nonwork trips, vehicle ownership changes, and other household members' behavior reshape the full household travel footprint after a switch to remote work.
status: Existing studies document context-dependent effects; avoided commuting alone is recognized as an incomplete endpoint. Key work: Cerqueira et al. (2020), *Does working from home reduce CO2 emissions? An analysis of travel patterns as dictated by workplaces*, DOI:10.1016/j.trd.2020.102338.
solved_when: A study measures total household travel and emissions — not just the avoided commute — capturing induced residential relocation, changes in nonwork trips, vehicle ownership, and other household members' travel behavior, and reports whether the net effect is a reduction or a rebound.
why: It determines whether remote work is an effective transportation decarbonization measure, since avoided commuting alone may be an incomplete endpoint if rebound effects offset the savings.
key_works: Cerqueira et al. (2020), *Does working from home reduce CO2 emissions? An analysis of travel patterns as dictated by workplaces*, DOI:10.1016/j.trd.2020.102338.

title: Built environment versus residential self-selection
subfield: Travel behavior, land use, and transport economics
open: Does neighborhood design itself cause people to travel differently, or do travelers choose neighborhoods that match how they already preferred to travel? A satisfying answer must isolate the causal effect of the built environment from residential self-selection — people's prior preferences, housing constraints, and relocation decisions.
status: Correlations between the built environment and travel are abundant, but transportable causal estimates remain a central land-use research need; see National Academies (2024), *Critical Issues in Transportation for 2024 and Beyond*, “Land Use,” DOI:10.17226/27432.
solved_when: A credible causal estimate of the effect of neighborhood design on travel behavior is obtained, with residential self-selection explicitly separated out.
why: It determines which urban-design interventions actually change travel behavior rather than merely sorting people who already behaved that way.
key_works: National Academies (2024), *Critical Issues in Transportation for 2024 and Beyond*, “Land Use,” DOI:10.17226/27432.

title: A sufficient-accessibility threshold
subfield: Travel behavior, land use, and transport economics
open: What level of access to jobs, care, education, and social activity is actually sufficient for a household to thrive, once individual constraints are accounted for? The task is to define and empirically validate such a sufficiency threshold for accessibility.
status: Accessibility measures exist, but a defensible sufficiency threshold is explicitly identified as unresolved, notably in National Academies (2024), *Critical Issues in Transportation for 2024 and Beyond*, "Promoting Equity and Inclusion."
solved_when: A defensible, validated sufficiency threshold for access to jobs, care, education, and social activity — incorporating individual constraints — is defined and supported by theory and empirical evidence.
why: It replaces the assumption that "more mobility is always better" with an outcome-based standard for transport planning and equity.
key_works: National Academies (2024), *Critical Issues in Transportation for 2024 and Beyond*, “Promoting Equity and Inclusion.”

title: Accessibility gains without displacement
subfield: Travel behavior, land use, and transport economics
open: Can transport-and-housing interventions be designed so that accessibility gains reach a neighborhood's existing residents rather than triggering their displacement?
status: Coordinating land use and transport remains an identified governance and research problem (National Academies (2024), *Critical Issues in Transportation for 2024 and Beyond*, "Land Use"); project-level gains can conceal population replacement.
solved_when: A designed, funded intervention demonstrates improved access for existing residents without pricing those residents out of the improved area.
why: Without such designs, accessibility investments relocate their intended beneficiaries — project-level gains conceal population replacement.
key_works: National Academies (2024), *Critical Issues in Transportation for 2024 and Beyond*, “Land Use.”

title: Perceived danger versus experienced harassment
subfield: Travel behavior, land use, and transport economics
open: How do actual harassment risk, perceived risk, social restrictions, and avoidance behavior each separately constrain people's travel choices? Formally, can an experimental design disentangle these distinct mechanisms and quantify their separate effects on travel and related decisions?
status: Research links perceived street risk to consequential educational decisions; distinguishing mechanisms remains essential for intervention design. Borker (2021), *Safety First: Perceived Risk of Street Harassment and Educational Choices of Women*, World Bank Policy Research Working Paper 9731.
solved_when: A study credibly identifies the separate causal effects of actual harassment risk, perceived risk, social restrictions, and avoidance behavior on travel choices, rather than their joint or confounded association.
why: Recorded incidents miss trips never attempted, so intervention design based on incident data alone cannot see the full set of constraints.
key_works: Borker (2021), *Safety First: Perceived Risk of Street Harassment and Educational Choices of Women*, World Bank Policy Research Working Paper 9731.

title: Politically durable mode-shift packages
subfield: Travel behavior, land use, and transport economics
open: What packages of service improvements, street redesign, pricing, and compensation can deliver substantial, sustained mode shift without resting on politically unattainable assumptions such as steep fuel or carbon taxes?
status: The National Academies' 2024 research agenda explicitly asks how large mode shifts can be achieved without steep fuel or carbon taxes. Key work: National Academies (2024), *Critical Issues in Transportation for 2024 and Beyond*, research appendix.
solved_when: A demonstrated combination of these measures produces substantial and sustained mode shift under realistic political constraints, with no requirement for politically unattainable assumptions.
why: Technically efficient policies are ineffective when they are repeatedly reversed; durability is what makes mode-shift gains stick.
key_works: National Academies (2024), *Critical Issues in Transportation for 2024 and Beyond*, research appendix.

title: Harassment interventions that expand feasible opportunities
subfield: Travel behavior, land use, and transport economics
open: Do harassment-reduction interventions expand the set of destinations and activities women can actually choose, rather than only improving reported comfort among existing riders? Formally, do such interventions causally increase women's feasible travel opportunities, not just their stated satisfaction?
status: Opportunity costs of perceived danger have been measured; comparative causal evidence on remedies remains the target. Borker (2021), *Safety First: Perceived Risk of Street Harassment and Educational Choices of Women*, Working Paper 9731.
solved_when: An experimental evaluation demonstrates a causal increase in women's chosen destinations and activities attributable to a harassment intervention, beyond improvements in reported comfort among existing riders.
why: It links transportation safety interventions to downstream education and employment outcomes, showing whether safety is a binding constraint on women's opportunity.
key_works: Borker (2021), *Safety First: Perceived Risk of Street Harassment and Educational Choices of Women*, Working Paper 9731.

title: Endogenous platform-driver labor supply
subfield: Travel behavior, land use, and transport economics
open: How do platform drivers jointly decide how much to work, on which platform, in response to fares, waiting times, work flexibility, and expenses? The open question is to build and validate a model of endogenous labor supply in which participation and multi-platform choices respond to these factors together.
status: The value of flexible work has been estimated — see Chen, Chevalier, Rossi, and Oehlsen (2019), *The Value of Flexible Work: Evidence from Uber Drivers*, DOI:10.1086/702171 — but stable policy predictions require richer endogenous participation and multi-platform behavior.
solved_when: A model of driver labor supply incorporating fares, waiting time, work flexibility, expenses, and competing platforms is developed and empirically validated, yielding stable policy predictions.
why: Dispatch and pricing models often treat available labor as an external input; endogenizing participation and multi-platform behavior would make platform design and policy evaluation reflect actual driver responses.
key_works: Chen, Chevalier, Rossi, and Oehlsen (2019), *The Value of Flexible Work: Evidence from Uber Drivers*, DOI:10.1086/702171.

title: Causal safety in numbers
open: How much of the well-known drop in per-person collision risk as walking and cycling volumes grow is actually caused by driver adaptation, infrastructure change, or route selection, rather than by confounding factors? In formal terms, what is the causal decomposition of the "safety in numbers" association, and which components transfer across settings?
status: The association is longstanding, documented in Jacobsen (2003), *Safety in numbers: more walkers and bicyclists, safer walking and bicycling*, DOI:10.1136/ip.9.3.205, but its causal decomposition and transferability are not supplied by the original observational relationship.
solved_when: A causal decomposition quantifies the contribution of driver adaptation, infrastructure change, route selection, and other confounders to the observed per-person risk reduction, with evidence on which components transfer to new contexts.
why: The answer changes the predicted safety consequences of increasing walking or cycling: if the association is largely causal, mode-shift policies yield larger safety gains than if it reflects confounding or selection.
key_works: Jacobsen (2003), *Safety in numbers: more walkers and bicyclists, safer walking and bicycling*, DOI:10.1136/ip.9.3.205.

title: Exposure denominators for small mobility modes
open: How much do people actually travel by cycling, scooters, wheelchairs, and walking — in distance, time, trips, and interactions with other road users — and with what uncertainty? Formally, can we produce comparable exposure measures with quantified uncertainty estimates across these small mobility modes?
status: Micromobility safety assessments identify inconsistent exposure and injury data as obstacles to comparisons; key works include Yannis, Crist, and Petraki (2024), *Safer micromobility: technical background report*, and ITF (2024), *Safer Micromobility*.
solved_when: Distance, time, trip, and interaction exposure are measured for cycling, scooters, wheelchairs, and walking, each with comparable uncertainty estimates across modes.
why: Injury counts alone cannot establish whether one mode or intervention is safer; exposure denominators are what turn raw injury counts into comparable risk estimates.
key_works: Yannis, Crist, and Petraki (2024), *Safer micromobility: technical background report*; ITF (2024), *Safer Micromobility*.

title: Transferable crossing-treatment effects
open: Can we predict, before installation, whether a given crossing treatment will be effective at a specific new location? More formally, given site characteristics such as vehicle speeds, pedestrian populations, visibility, turning movements, and compliance, can treatment effects be reliably transferred to that site?
status: Pedestrian hybrid beacons are an established countermeasure (FHWA, *Pedestrian Hybrid Beacons*, Proven Safety Countermeasures program), but reliable local treatment-effect prediction is a stronger requirement that has not been met.
solved_when: A validated predictive method exists that forecasts the local effect of crossing interventions from site-level variables (vehicle speeds, pedestrian populations, visibility, turning movements, and compliance) with demonstrated reliability at new locations.
why: It would let agencies spend retrofit budgets where treatments will actually work, instead of applying uniform installation rules that waste resources at sites where the countermeasure fails.
key_works: FHWA, *Pedestrian Hybrid Beacons*, Proven Safety Countermeasures program.

title: Micromobility geometry and injury severity
open: How do the physical design choices of micromobility vehicles — wheel size, steering geometry, braking, and rider posture — determine injury severity when riders encounter real road defects? The goal is to establish validated relationships linking these design and posture variables to injury outcomes in actual crash and near-crash conditions.
status: Vehicle-design recommendations already exist, but comparable crash and near-crash evidence across different designs remains limited. ITF (2024), *Safer Micromobility*, DOI:10.1787/0d2e0dd5-en.
solved_when: Validated, empirically grounded relationships exist between wheel size, steering geometry, braking, rider posture, and injury outcomes, supported by comparable crash and near-crash evidence across different vehicle designs.
why: Such relationships would allow injuries to be reduced through vehicle design, rather than relying solely on rider behavior.
key_works: ITF (2024), *Safer Micromobility*, DOI:10.1787/0d2e0dd5-en.

title: Nighttime micromobility conspicuity
open: Which lighting and conspicuity designs make nighttime micromobility riders more detectable while also supporting accurate judgments of their speed? The target is configurations that improve detection and correct speed judgment without producing glare or otherwise misleading visual cues.
status: Safety guidance addresses visibility, but performance across road layouts, weather, and rider populations remains an experimental target. ITF (2024), *Safer Micromobility*, DOI:10.1787/0d2e0dd5-en.
solved_when: An experimental demonstration identifies lighting/conspicuity designs that measurably improve detection and correct speed judgment, without introducing glare or misleading cues, across varied road layouts, weather conditions, and rider populations.
why: Being noticed is not equivalent to being perceived accurately — a rider who is seen but whose speed is misjudged remains at risk.
key_works: ITF (2024), *Safer Micromobility*, DOI:10.1787/0d2e0dd5-en.

title: Micromobility near-miss metrics that predict injury
open: Do near-miss metrics derived from video conflict analysis actually predict future serious injuries in micromobility, and do those relationships hold across different modes and street designs?
status: Surrogate indicators offer faster feedback than crash counts, but require mode-specific validation. Key works: Yannis, Crist, and Petraki (2024), *Safer micromobility: technical background report*.
solved_when: Video-derived conflict indicators are validated against future serious-injury outcomes across distinct micromobility modes and street design contexts, demonstrating predictive value rather than mere correlation with convenience metrics.
why: Without validation, planners risk optimizing a convenient proxy that does not track actual harm, misdirecting safety investments.
key_works: Yannis, Crist, and Petraki (2024), *Safer micromobility: technical background report*.

title: Transient sidewalk obstruction mapping
open: Can temporary sidewalk barriers—parked scooters, construction, deliveries, snow—be detected and mapped quickly enough that accessible routing updates before travelers reach the obstruction? Formally: how can transient obstructions be detected, localized, and propagated into route computations at the timescale on which they appear and disappear?
status: Large-scale accessibility inventories exist—e.g., Saha et al. (2019), *Project Sidewalk: A Web-based Crowdsourcing Tool for Collecting Sidewalk Accessibility Data at Scale*, DOI:10.1145/3290605.3300292—but transient conditions remain harder to capture than persistent curb and pavement defects.
solved_when: A system continuously detects transient sidewalk obstructions and updates accessible route information before travelers would encounter the blockage; since no quantitative targets (detection rates, latency budgets, coverage sizes) are stated in the record, the natural criterion is that route updates propagate within the effective lifetime of a typical transient obstruction.
why: A nominally accessible route can become unusable within minutes, so static accessibility inventories silently fail exactly when a traveler depends on them.
key_works: Saha et al. (2019), *Project Sidewalk: A Web-based Crowdsourcing Tool for Collecting Sidewalk Accessibility Data at Scale*, DOI:10.1145/3290605.3300292.

title: Marginal value of a missing active-travel link
open: What is the marginal value of completing a specific missing link in an active-travel network — how much does it change participation and safety, including trips that were previously suppressed entirely? Formally, this asks for an estimate of the causal effect of closing an individual network gap on cycling and walking behaviour and injury risk, accounting for induced and previously suppressed trips.
status: Network-wide exposure and safety relationships are known — Jacobsen (2003), *Safety in numbers: more walkers and bicyclists, safer walking and bicycling*, established that more walkers and bicyclists make walking and bicycling safer — but individual-link effects remain poorly understood, as they are nonlinear and context-dependent.
solved_when: A method or study exists that credibly estimates, for a specific link completion, the change in active-travel participation (including previously suppressed trips) and the change in risk, with the nonlinear, context-dependent nature of individual-link effects characterized rather than assumed away.
why: A short connection can matter more than a much longer disconnected facility, so planners cannot rank infrastructure investments by length alone; without credible link-level estimates, network investment decisions systematically misallocate resources.
key_works: Jacobsen (2003), *Safety in numbers: more walkers and bicyclists, safer walking and bicycling*.

title: Tenfold longer useful micromobility service
open: Can the useful passenger-kilometers delivered per manufactured shared scooter be increased tenfold over a specified baseline, without shifting burdens into maintenance or collection operations?
status: Lifecycle work identifies manufacturing and fleet servicing as important contributors to scooter environmental impact; the tenfold target requires whole-system validation. Hollingsworth, Copeland, and Johnson (2019), *Are e-scooters polluters?*, DOI:10.1088/1748-9326/ab2da8.
solved_when: A whole-system validation demonstrates a tenfold increase in useful passenger-kilometers per manufactured scooter against the specified baseline, with no burden shifted to maintenance or collection.
why: Durability improvements may outperform incremental battery-efficiency gains, cutting the manufacturing and servicing impacts that dominate scooter lifecycles.
key_works: Hollingsworth, Copeland, and Johnson (2019), *Are e-scooters polluters?*, DOI:10.1088/1748-9326/ab2da8.

title: Reliability of the complete accessible journey
subfield: Accessibility, disability, and complete trip chains
open: Can we predict whether a traveler's complete journey remains feasible when any of its links — sidewalks, elevators, vehicles, boarding interfaces, and assistance services — may fail at any point along the way? Formally, this asks for a model of end-to-end trip reliability that captures dependencies and time-varying states across all components of the chain.
status: Current accessibility inventories, such as Saha et al. (2019), *Project Sidewalk*, DOI:10.1145/3290605.3300292, address individual barriers; end-to-end reliability requires modeling their dependencies and changing states, which remains undone. Related theory exists in reliability of series systems and dependent component failure.
solved_when: A method exists that predicts feasibility of an entire trip chain from accessibility inventory data, accounting for dependencies and changing states among sidewalks, elevators, vehicles, boarding interfaces, and assistance services.
why: A single failed segment can invalidate every otherwise accessible component of a journey, so trip-level prediction is what actually determines whether a traveler gets through.
key_works: Saha et al. (2019), *Project Sidewalk*, DOI:10.1145/3290605.3300292.

title: Uncertainty-aware accessibility attributes
subfield: Accessibility, disability, and complete trip chains
open: Can we attach calibrated uncertainty estimates to sidewalk attributes — slope, width, curb condition, surface quality, and obstructions — and propagate that uncertainty through to personalized route recommendations? Formally, the goal is a pipeline in which per-attribute confidence is statistically calibrated and routes respect each user's tolerance for risk.
status: Large image galleries and crowdsourced labels already exist — e.g., Duan et al. (2021), *Sidewalk Gallery: An Interactive, Filterable Image Gallery of Over 500,000 Sidewalk Accessibility Problems* — but no approach yet makes the resulting uncertainty meaningful to users with different tolerances. Related directions include uncertainty calibration and personalized risk constraints.
solved_when: Slope, width, curb condition, surface quality, and obstruction labels each carry calibrated uncertainty, and that uncertainty demonstrably shapes route recommendations in a way users with different tolerances can act on.
why: Overconfident accessibility information can strand travelers — someone told a route is wheelchair-navigable when it is not may be left stuck mid-trip.
key_works: Duan et al. (2021), *Sidewalk Gallery: An Interactive, Filterable Image Gallery of Over 500,000 Sidewalk Accessibility Problems*.

title: Turning accessibility reports into repairs
subfield: Accessibility, disability, and complete trip chains
open: Which institutional and funding arrangements reliably convert reports of accessibility barriers into verified repairs, without systematically favoring neighborhoods with greater reporting capacity? More precisely, can experimental evaluation identify governance and budget structures under which remediation outcomes track actual barrier prevalence rather than complaint volume?
status: Accessibility has been analyzed as a sociopolitical problem; data collection alone does not establish effective remediation. Saha et al. (2020), *Urban Accessibility as a Socio-Political Problem: A Multi-Stakeholder Analysis*.
solved_when: Arrangements are identified and experimentally validated that reliably turn reported barriers into verified repairs while avoiding bias toward high-reporting neighborhoods; the criterion applies to complete trip chains.
why: An accurate map of barriers is not the same as an accessible city — data collection alone does not establish effective remediation.
key_works: Saha et al. (2020), *Urban Accessibility as a Socio-Political Problem: A Multi-Stakeholder Analysis*.

title: Wheelchair-inclusive aircraft emergency procedures
subfield: Accessibility, disability, and complete trip chains
open: Can aircraft evacuation and emergency-response procedures be validated as safe for passengers who remain in their own wheelchairs, including in constrained aisles and when crew assistance is unavailable? A complete answer requires experimental and engineering evidence covering such scenarios end-to-end.
status: Preliminary feasibility work has been done — National Academies (2021), *Technical Feasibility of a Wheelchair Securement Concept for Airline Travel*, DOI:10.17226/26323 — but it does not close all operational and emergency integration questions.
solved_when: Validated evacuation and emergency-response procedures exist for wheelchair-remaining passengers, demonstrated under constrained-aisle and no-assistance conditions, closing the remaining operational and emergency-integration questions.
why: Accessibility must remain safe outside normal boarding and cruising; without validated procedures, inclusive air travel breaks down precisely in the moments when safety is most at risk.
key_works: National Academies (2021), *Technical Feasibility of a Wheelchair Securement Concept for Airline Travel*, DOI:10.17226/26323.

title: Reliable dynamic paratransit insertion
subfield: Accessibility, disability, and complete trip chains
open: Can a paratransit system accept new ride requests and cancellations in real time while still guaranteeing each rider's individual ride-time, assistance, vehicle-compatibility, and appointment constraints? Formally, the goal is a dynamic insertion procedure for dial-a-ride operations that maintains per-rider constraint satisfaction, not just aggregate efficiency, under continuous updates.
status: Dial-a-ride optimization is mature in many formulations, as surveyed by Cordeau and Laporte (2007), *The dial-a-ride problem: models and algorithms*, DOI:10.1007/s10479-007-0170-8; however, robust real-time service across these combined constraints remains a deployment target.
solved_when: A real-time insertion and cancellation handling mechanism is demonstrated that preserves every individual ride-time, assistance, vehicle-compatibility, and appointment constraint; since the record states no explicit quantitative budget, success is achieving robust dynamic service across all these combined constraints in deployment-scale operation.
why: Average efficiency can conceal unacceptable service for riders with complex needs, so without such a mechanism optimization gains come at the expense of the riders the service exists for.
key_works: Cordeau and Laporte (2007), *The dial-a-ride problem: models and algorithms*, DOI:10.1007/s10479-007-0170-8.

title: Recovery after an accessible connection fails
subfield: Accessibility, disability, and complete trip chains
open: When an elevator breaks, a vehicle fails to arrive, a transfer falls through, or a booked support service is not delivered, can the system replan and actually deliver the assistance the traveler needs — with a guaranteed bound on abandonment and delay?
status: Route optimization and accessibility mapping provide useful components, but coordinated recovery across operators remains a stronger target than current practice. Key works include Cordeau and Laporte (2007), *The dial-a-ride problem*, and the Project Sidewalk research program.
solved_when: A recovery procedure exists that, upon failure of any elevator, vehicle, transfer, or booked support service, produces and executes a new accessible plan delivering the required assistance, with a proven bound on both abandonment and delay.
why: Accessible travel depends on dependable recovery when things fail, not merely on an optimistic plan made before the trip begins.
key_works: Cordeau and Laporte (2007), *The dial-a-ride problem*; Project Sidewalk research program.

title: Measuring disability-related suppressed travel
subfield: Accessibility, disability, and complete trip chains
open: How many trips do people with disabilities want to make but do not, because of disability-related barriers? A satisfying method would estimate these forgone trips and forgone opportunities while distinguishing genuinely suppressed demand from voluntary nontravel.
status: National travel surveys document realized travel differences; unrealized desired journeys are harder to observe. Key work: Bureau of Transportation Statistics (2026 update), *Travel Patterns of American Adults with Disabilities*, using the 2022 National Household Travel Survey.
solved_when: A measurement approach yields estimates of trips and opportunities forgone due to disability-related barriers that credibly separate unmet demand from voluntary nontravel.
why: Counting only completed trips understates exclusion, since people deterred by barriers never appear in travel data at all.
key_works: Bureau of Transportation Statistics (2026 update), *Travel Patterns of American Adults with Disabilities*, using the 2022 National Household Travel Survey.

title: Cognitive accessibility of trip execution
subfield: Accessibility, disability, and complete trip chains
open: Do independently completed journeys become measurably more achievable for travelers with cognitive, sensory, and communication disabilities when booking tools, wayfinding, transfers, and disruption messages are redesigned? Formally, this asks for experimental validation that specific interface changes across the full trip chain improve independent trip execution for these populations.
status: Aggregate disability travel statistics, such as those in the Bureau of Transportation Statistics' *Travel Patterns of American Adults with Disabilities*, 2026 update, do not identify which interface changes close which execution barriers.
solved_when: Empirical evidence demonstrates, through independently completed journeys as the endpoint, that validated changes to booking, wayfinding, transfer, and disruption-message interfaces reduce execution barriers for people with differing cognitive, sensory, and communication needs.
why: Physical accessibility alone does not make a trip independently usable; without knowing which interface changes close which execution barriers, travelers who cannot independently execute a trip remain excluded despite compliant infrastructure.
key_works: Bureau of Transportation Statistics, *Travel Patterns of American Adults with Disabilities*, 2026 update.

title: Passenger-optimal bus-bunching control
open: Can transit agencies hold or dispatch buses in a way that is provably good for passengers — not merely for headway regularity — by weighing riders already onboard, those waiting at stops, in-vehicle crowding, and downstream transfer connections in a single objective?
status: Headway-based anti-bunching control is established, notably via Daganzo (2009), *A headway-based approach to eliminate bus bunching: Systematic analysis and comparisons*; passenger-level objectives introduce additional trade-offs beyond what headway regularity captures.
solved_when: A control strategy is specified that jointly accounts for onboard passengers, waiting passengers, crowding, and downstream transfers, together with an analysis (analytical or empirical) demonstrating its passenger-level performance against headway-regularity-only baselines.
why: Holding a bus can help future riders while harming current ones, so a control law blind to passenger states can systematically sacrifice the very people it is meant to serve.
key_works: Daganzo (2009), *A headway-based approach to eliminate bus bunching: Systematic analysis and comparisons*.

title: Transfer-aware cooperation between buses
open: Can intersecting bus routes coordinate their holding decisions so that transfers are protected, without introducing cascading missed connections or destabilizing headway regularity on either route?
status: Bus-to-bus cooperation, as in Daganzo and Pilachowski (2011), *Reducing bunching with bus-to-bus cooperation*, addresses bunching, but network-wide transfer dependencies require broader coordination.
solved_when: A control scheme for holding across intersecting routes is specified and shown to maintain transfer synchronisation while avoiding cascading missed connections and preserving stable headways on each individual route.
why: Even a route that is locally regular can produce unreliable door-to-door journeys when transfers fail; solving this makes network-level journey reliability achievable.
key_works: Daganzo and Pilachowski (2011), *Reducing bunching with bus-to-bus cooperation*.

title: Bunching with denied boarding
open: Can transit service be stabilized when full vehicles deny boarding, so that left-behind passengers accumulate into queues that lengthen future dwell times and intensify boarding demand at later stops? A satisfying answer would characterize the coupled dynamics of headways, vehicle loads, and waiting queues under capacity saturation, and show how to keep the system stable despite this feedback.
status: Classical holding analyses provide the foundations, following Daganzo (2009), *A headway-based approach to eliminate bus bunching*; capacity saturation, however, introduces an additional positive feedback that those analyses do not address.
solved_when: A model and control policy are given that provably stabilize headways and passenger queues on a saturated corridor, with stability conditions explicit in the feedback loop between denied boarding, dwell times, and boarding demand.
why: The busiest services are often those least well represented by unconstrained boarding models, so current bunching theory leaves exactly the most crowded routes without reliable analysis or control.
key_works: Daganzo (2009), *A headway-based approach to eliminate bus bunching*.

title: Joint transit route, frequency, and timetable design
open: Can we design a full transit network for an entire city — routes, frequencies, and timetables together — while properly accounting for how passengers reroute and for uncertainty in demand and operations?
