In formal terms, the challenge is a city-scale optimization problem whose decision variables span network design, service frequencies, and schedules, coupled with passenger reassignment and stochastic elements.
status: Extensive decomposition and optimization methods already exist, but integration, scale, and realistic passenger behavior remain competing demands that current approaches trade off against one another. A global review of the field is Guihaire and Hao (2008), *Transit network design and scheduling: A global review*, DOI:10.1016/j.tra.2008.03.011.
solved_when: A method exists that solves the joint route, frequency, and timetable design problem at city scale, with passenger reassignment and uncertainty explicitly represented in the model.
why: When routes, frequencies, and timetables are optimized in separate stages, each stage can undo the benefits of the others; a joint solution avoids this mutual degradation.
key_works: Guihaire and Hao (2008), *Transit network design and scheduling: A global review*, DOI:10.1016/j.tra.2008.03.011.

title: Service guarantees for pooled demand-responsive transit
open: What level of service can a pooled demand-responsive transit system actually guarantee its riders? Formally, determine the achievable trade-offs between vehicle productivity, maximum wait, detour, rejection probability, and equitable coverage under uncertain requests.
status: Dial-a-ride algorithms address many variants of the problem, but universally favorable pooling claims are not supported without demand and service assumptions. Key work: Cordeau and Laporte (2007), *The dial-a-ride problem: models and algorithms*.
solved_when: A characterization (theoretical or experimental) of the trade-off frontier between vehicle productivity, maximum wait, detour, rejection probability, and equitable coverage is established under specified demand and service assumptions for uncertain requests.
why: It clarifies when pooling is genuinely useful rather than merely cheap for the operator.
key_works: Cordeau and Laporte (2007), *The dial-a-ride problem: models and algorithms*.

title: Fixed-route versus flexible-service transition thresholds
open: At what demand densities and demand variabilities should an operator abandon fixed-route bus service in favor of feeder or fully demand-responsive service? The goal is to identify empirically validated thresholds at which each service mode becomes the better choice.
status: Transit design methods, surveyed in Guihaire and Hao (2008), *Transit network design and scheduling: A global review*, provide alternatives, but the transition thresholds depend on geography, service guarantees, and endogenous demand.
solved_when: Empirically validated demand-density and variability thresholds exist that specify when to switch among fixed routes, feeders, and demand-responsive service, accounting for geography, service guarantees, and endogenous demand.
why: Without such thresholds, operators risk replacing productive buses with inefficient small vehicles, or running nearly empty fixed routes indefinitely.
key_works: Guihaire and Hao (2008), *Transit network design and scheduling: A global review*.

title: Integrated electric-bus scheduling under disruption
open: Can a transit operator recover its full operations plan — timetable, vehicle assignments, charging, and driver duties — in a single integrated process after a disruption such as a delay or charger failure, while still preserving passenger service?
status: Integrated timetabling and vehicle scheduling has been demonstrated; electrification adds energy and infrastructure dependencies. Key work: Ibarra-Rojas, Giesen, and Rios-Solis (2014), *An integrated approach for timetabling and vehicle scheduling problems to analyze the trade-off between level of service and operating costs of transit networks*.
solved_when: A method exists that jointly recovers timetables, vehicle assignments, charging schedules, and driver duties after delays or charger failures and preserves passenger service.
why: A feasible timetable is useless when assigned vehicles cannot charge or drivers cannot legally operate it; integration is what keeps the recovery plan actually executable.
key_works: Ibarra-Rojas, Giesen, and Rios-Solis (2014), *An integrated approach for timetabling and vehicle scheduling problems to analyze the trade-off between level of service and operating costs of transit networks*.

title: Incentive-compatible through-ticketing
open: How should fares be integrated and revenue shared among independent transit operators so that reliable transfers and broad coverage are rewarded, while no operator is incentivized to turn away unprofitable connecting passengers?
status: Integrated ticketing exists, but aligned incentives across independent operators remain a governance problem. Key work: National Academies (2024), *Critical Issues in Transportation for 2024 and Beyond*, "Governance."
solved_when: A fare-integration and revenue-sharing mechanism is specified that is incentive-compatible — operators participate and accept connecting passengers under the sharing rule — while sustaining reliable transfers and coverage across independent operators.
why: Payment interoperability alone does not create an integrated service; without aligned incentives, through-ticketing breaks down at the operator boundary.
key_works: National Academies (2024), *Critical Issues in Transportation for 2024 and Beyond*, “Governance.”

title: Stable funding for useful transit operations
open: How can transit agencies secure funding mechanisms that sustain useful service frequency and maintenance through demand shocks, rather than disproportionately favoring new capital projects?
status: The mismatch between operating needs and available funding remains an identified institutional problem, as noted in National Academies (2024), *Critical Issues in Transportation for 2024 and Beyond*, "Funding and Finance."
solved_when: A funding mechanism exists that maintains dependable service frequency and maintenance levels through demand shocks, with operating needs funded on par with or ahead of new capital projects.
why: Infrastructure delivers little value without dependable service; without stable operating support, capital investments sit idle while ridership suffers.
key_works: National Academies (2024), *Critical Issues in Transportation for 2024 and Beyond*, “Funding and Finance.”

title: Transit rosters that retain workers
open: How do split shifts, schedule predictability, recovery time, and route assignments shape transit-worker retention and the reliability of the service they deliver? The goal is to quantify these effects and then use them to design rosters that optimize both retention and reliability.
status: Workforce shortages and skill needs are documented — see National Academies (2024), *Critical Issues in Transportation for 2024 and Beyond*, "Workforce" — but causal evidence on the best operational remedies remains incomplete.
solved_when: Causal evidence identifies how split shifts, schedule predictability, recovery time, and route assignments affect retention and service reliability, and rostering methods exist that optimize these operational levers for both outcomes.
why: Nominal fleet capacity does not become service without a sustainable workforce; agencies cannot run their timetables if rosters drive workers out.
key_works: National Academies (2024), *Critical Issues in Transportation for 2024 and Beyond*, “Workforce.”

title: Certifiable virtual coupling
open: Can trains that brake cooperatively, rather than each guarding a fixed block, be allowed to run close enough together to matter — and still be certified safe? Formally, the goal is to establish a certifiable operating envelope for virtually coupled trains that explicitly accounts for communication faults and heterogeneous onboard equipment.
status: Reviews through 2026 describe substantial control development, but deployment still requires integration with safety assurance and railway operations practice; see Félez and Vaquero-Serrano (2023), *Virtual Coupling in Railways: A Comprehensive Review*, DOI:10.3390/machines11050521, and Zhang et al. (2026), DOI:10.1007/s40864-026-00277-9.
solved_when: A defined operating envelope exists under which close-following virtually coupled operation is certified safe, with the envelope explicitly covering communication faults and heterogeneous equipment, and validated through integration with safety assurance and railway operations.
why: It would raise line capacity without constructing equivalent additional track, turning coordination software into a substitute for civil infrastructure.
key_works: Félez and Vaquero-Serrano (2023), *Virtual Coupling in Railways: A Comprehensive Review*, DOI:10.3390/machines11050521; Zhang et al. (2026), DOI:10.1007/s40864-026-00277-9.

title: Virtual coupling through junctions
open: Can virtually coupled train groups be safely formed, split, and rerouted through junctions — switches and stations — without losing the headway advantage that virtual coupling exists to provide? Formally, this asks for coordination and verification mechanisms for topology-changing operations that preserve safety guarantees across the coupling transition.
status: Following control is only one component of the problem; topology-changing operations such as those at junctions require additional coordination and verification, which remains unresolved. Zhang et al. (2026), *A Comprehensive Review of Virtually Coupled Train Systems*, DOI:10.1007/s40864-026-00277-9, surveys the area.
solved_when: A scheme exists that safely forms, splits, and reroutes virtual train groups around switches and stations while retaining the headway benefits of virtual coupling, with the required coordination and verification for topology-changing operations demonstrated.
why: Railway capacity is often constrained by junctions rather than plain track, so a virtual coupling scheme that breaks down at junctions would forfeit its capacity gains exactly where they matter most.
key_works: Zhang et al. (2026), *A Comprehensive Review of Virtually Coupled Train Systems*, DOI:10.1007/s40864-026-00277-9.

title: Heterogeneous braking in closely spaced trains
open: How can we certify safe following distances between closely spaced trains whose braking behavior differs — accounting for load, adhesion, brake degradation, and uncertain response times across unlike vehicles?
status: Robust control approaches exist, but dependable bounds for heterogeneous operational fleets remain a demanding target; see Félez and Vaquero-Serrano (2023), *Virtual Coupling in Railways: A Comprehensive Review*.
solved_when: A method exists that yields dependable, certified bounds on safe following distance for heterogeneous operational fleets, explicitly incorporating load, adhesion, brake degradation, and uncertain response times.
why: A following train cannot assume the leader shares its braking capabilities, so distance guarantees derived from homogeneous assumptions are unsound in mixed fleets.
key_works: Félez and Vaquero-Serrano (2023), *Virtual Coupling in Railways: A Comprehensive Review*.

title: Local low-adhesion forecasting
open: Can short-lived patches of low rail adhesion — caused by localized contamination and weather — be forecast at a spatial and temporal resolution fine enough to matter for braking, before trains actually reach them? Formally, the goal is prediction of localized low-adhesion events ahead of encounter, at braking-relevant granularity.
status: Adhesion research remains an active railway program (RSSB, *Adhesion Research Group* research program); however, localized contamination and weather make network-wide prediction difficult, and no local forecasting capability at braking-relevant resolution is established.
solved_when: A forecasting method reliably predicts short-lived low-adhesion patches before train arrival, at spatial and temporal resolution sufficient for braking decisions under operating conditions.
why: Accurate local forecasts would directly improve braking safety and timetable reliability, since adhesion loss is both a safety hazard and a source of delays.
key_works: RSSB, *Adhesion Research Group* research program.

title: Wheel–rail friction under thin contamination layers
open: Can we predict and experimentally reproduce the friction transitions that small amounts of water and mixed contaminants cause in the wheel–rail contact, across realistic ranges of load, speed, and surface history?
status: Full-scale experiments have demonstrated important low-adhesion effects — notably in Buckley-Johnstone et al. (2020), *Full-scale testing of low adhesion effects with small amounts of water in the wheel/rail interface* — but general predictive friction maps remain the target.
solved_when: A predictive friction map is established and validated against full-scale experiments that covers the friction transitions induced by small quantities of water and mixed contaminants across load, speed, and surface histories.
why: Small environmental changes can produce disproportionately large braking changes, so reliable prediction directly bears on braking safety and performance.
key_works: Buckley-Johnstone et al. (2020), *Full-scale testing of low adhesion effects with small amounts of water in the wheel/rail interface*.

title: Non-destructive ballast moisture and fouling inference
open: Can subsurface fouling and retained water in railway ballast be inferred non-destructively from affordable, practical inspections? In particular, can such inference be made to transfer reliably across seasons, ballast types, and track structures?
status: Infrared thermography combined with statistical processing has shown promise for this task, as reported by Koohmishi, Gao, Jing, and Guo (2025), *Non-destructive assessment of railway ballast fouling and water retention using infrared thermography and statistical processing*, DOI:10.1016/j.conbuildmat.2025.140273, but transfer of these results across field conditions still requires validation.
solved_when: A non-destructive inspection method is demonstrated to infer subsurface fouling and retained water accurately across different seasons, ballast types, and track structures in field conditions.
why: Hidden deterioration governs drainage performance, settlement, and maintenance needs, so reliable inference would let maintenance be targeted before visible damage accumulates.
key_works: Koohmishi, Gao, Jing, and Guo (2025), *Non-destructive assessment of railway ballast fouling and water retention using infrared thermography and statistical processing*, DOI:10.1016/j.conbuildmat.2025.140273.

title: Causal prediction of tamping benefit
open: Can we predict not just when track geometry will deteriorate, but how each feasible tamping intervention would change future deterioration and total maintenance demand? Formally, this is the question of identifying intervention effects on degradation dynamics, a stronger requirement than forecasting untreated trends.
status: Current models predict future tamping requirements, as in Charoenwong et al. (2025), *Prediction of future railway ballast tamping requirements*, Transportation Geotechnics 55, 101652; identifying intervention effects remains a stronger, unmet requirement.
solved_when: A model exists that, for any feasible tamping intervention, predicts the resulting change in future track geometry deterioration and total maintenance demand — beyond predicting tamping requirements under current practice.
why: Repeated maintenance can alter the material whose behavior is being predicted, so forecasts that ignore intervention effects systematically misjudge future maintenance needs.
key_works: Charoenwong et al. (2025), *Prediction of future railway ballast tamping requirements*, Transportation Geotechnics 55, 101652.

title: Transferable corrugation-maintenance selection
open: How should maintenance decision-makers select combinations of rail grinding, friction management, and vehicle–track modifications that durably and cost-effectively control corrugation, in a way that transfers across the different mechanisms that produce it? Formally, the goal is a transferable lifecycle-level selection method for intervention packages matched to corrugation mechanism.
status: Corrugation mechanisms and their treatments are extensively understood — Grassie (2009), *Rail corrugation: Characteristics, causes, and treatments*, DOI:10.1243/09544097JRRT264 — so the open target is transferable lifecycle intervention selection, not explaining corrugation from scratch. Related directions include mechanism-specific maintenance and lifecycle optimization.
solved_when: A method exists for choosing durable, cost-effective combinations of grinding, friction management, and vehicle–track changes that demonstrably transfers across different corrugation mechanisms and supports lifecycle-level optimization of interventions.
why: Repeatedly removing corrugation damage without addressing its underlying cause wastes maintenance resources; a transferable selection method would direct spending at mechanisms rather than symptoms.
key_works: Grassie (2009), *Rail corrugation: Characteristics, causes, and treatments*, DOI:10.1243/09544097JRRT264.

title: Coordinated digital automatic coupling rollout
open: How can the rollout of digital automatic coupling across a rail fleet be financed, sequenced, and standardized so that conversion is viable even while mixed-equipped trains run and the benefits are spread across many actors?
status: Investment planning exists, but network effects and transitional incompatibilities remain central deployment barriers. Key work: Europe’s Rail (2023), *European DAC Investment Plan*.
solved_when: A concrete set of financing, sequencing, and interoperability arrangements exists under which fleet conversion becomes viable despite mixed-equipped trains and distributed benefits among actors.
why: Individually rational delayed adoption can prevent a beneficial network transition, so without coordinated arrangements the fleet may never convert.
key_works: Europe’s Rail (2023), *European DAC Investment Plan*.

title: Route-specific replacement of diesel rail traction
open: How should a railway choose, route by route, among electrification, battery, and other low-emission traction options so that the choice is defensible against real operating conditions? The question is to select and validate traction portfolios using whole-route duty cycles, infrastructure, resilience, and lifecycle impacts.
status: Multiple technologies and demonstrations exist, but no single option dominates every lightly used or remote route. Related effort: Europe's Rail, *RAIL4EARTH—A sustainable and green rail system*.
solved_when: A validated route-specific method exists for selecting and demonstrating low-emission traction portfolios, evaluating candidate technologies against whole-route duty cycles, infrastructure constraints, resilience, and lifecycle impacts, with demonstrations confirming the selections on lightly used or remote routes where no single option dominates.
why: It prevents an unsuitable decarbonization technology from being forced onto an entire railway, allowing decarbonization choices to match each route's actual conditions.
key_works: Europe’s Rail, *RAIL4EARTH—A sustainable and green rail system*.

title: Truthful collaborative freight pooling
subfield: Freight, urban logistics, and cold chains
open: When multiple carriers pool freight capacity and share the resulting savings, can the allocation be designed so that no carrier gains by misreporting its demand, costs, availability, or service quality? Formally, this asks for a mechanism for collaborative freight pooling in which truthful reporting is a dominant strategy (or an equilibrium) while capacity and savings are allocated efficiently.
status: Open logistics architectures such as the Physical Internet motivate pooling — see Montreuil (2011), *Toward a Physical Internet: Meeting the Global Logistics Sustainability Grand Challenge*, DOI:10.1007/s12159-011-0045-x — but the literature does not yet establish that these gains translate into incentive-compatible participation; no truthful mechanism for this setting is known.
solved_when: A mechanism is specified for shared-capacity and savings allocation in carrier coalitions, together with a proof that truthful reporting of demand, costs, availability, and service quality is incentive-compatible, and that the resulting allocation is stable against coalitional deviations.
why: Operational gains from pooling do not by themselves make participation rational; collaboration collapses when carriers profit from withholding or distorting information, so incentive compatibility is what makes shared-logistics architectures actually work.
key_works: Montreuil (2011), *Toward a Physical Internet: Meeting the Global Logistics Sustainability Grand Challenge*, DOI:10.1007/s12159-011-0045-x.

title: Interoperable Physical Internet handling
subfield: Freight, urban logistics, and cold chains
open: Can modular freight units, handling equipment, identification schemes, and routing be made interoperable across independently operated networks, so that freight moves through shared infrastructure without excessive repacking or wasteful circulation of empty units?
status: The Physical Internet supplies an architectural vision — Montreuil (2011), *Toward a Physical Internet*, DOI:10.1007/s12159-011-0045-x — but universal operational compatibility remains a larger engineering target not yet achieved.
solved_when: A system of modular freight units, handling equipment, identification, and routing is demonstrated to operate compatibly across independent networks, with repacking and empty-unit circulation kept to levels that are not excessive (i.e., operationally acceptable rather than a specified numeric budget, as none is stated).
why: It would let freight flow through shared networks instead of isolated company systems, which is the core practical payoff of the Physical Internet vision.
key_works: Montreuil (2011), *Toward a Physical Internet*, DOI:10.1007/s12159-011-0045-x.

title: Real-world value of pooled human–robot logistics
subfield: Freight, urban logistics, and cold chains
open: Does pooling human and robot resources dynamically in urban parcel logistics actually reduce total delivery cost in the real world, while preserving worker safety and service quality when disruptions occur? Formally, this calls for a field demonstration — not just a model — of dynamic human–robot resource pooling under real operational disruptions.
status: A 2026 study develops dynamic deployment models for pooled human–robot resources, but sustained field performance remains a separate, unmet validation target. Key work: Xu, Klibi, and Montreuil (2026), *Dynamic deployment of pooled human-robot resources in urban parcel logistics*, DOI:10.1016/j.trb.2026.103409.
solved_when: A sustained field validation shows that dynamic human–robot resource pooling reduces total delivery cost relative to the non-pooled baseline while maintaining worker safety and service quality under real disruptions.
why: Simulated gains in labor or robot utilization can disappear during actual execution, so without field evidence operators cannot know whether pooling delivers real value.
key_works: Xu, Klibi, and Montreuil (2026), *Dynamic deployment of pooled human-robot resources in urban parcel logistics*, DOI:10.1016/j.trb.2026.103409.

title: Joint curb allocation and delivery routing
subfield: Freight, urban logistics, and cold chains
open: Can delivery routes be optimized jointly with the time-varying legal stopping capacity of curbs, together with pedestrian access, congestion, and enforcement uncertainty? In formal terms, the question asks for an integrated model in which routing decisions and curb allocation are decision variables coupled under stochastic, time-dependent constraints.
status: Existing city-logistics methods address routing and consolidation, but the curb is typically treated as freely available rather than as a contested resource; see Savelsbergh and Van Woensel (2016), *50th Anniversary Invited Article—City Logistics: Challenges and Opportunities*, DOI:10.1287/trsc.2016.0675.
solved_when: A joint optimization framework exists that treats curb space as a time-varying, contested resource — accounting for legal stopping capacity, pedestrian access, congestion, and enforcement uncertainty — and produces routes whose operational feasibility is guaranteed rather than assumed.
why: A route can be geographically short yet operationally infeasible; without such a model, planners optimize distance while ignoring whether vehicles can actually stop and deliver.
key_works: Savelsbergh and Van Woensel (2016), *50th Anniversary Invited Article—City Logistics: Challenges and Opportunities*, DOI:10.1287/trsc.2016.0675.

title: Causal net benefit of urban microhubs
subfield: Freight, urban logistics, and cold chains
open: Does an urban microhub actually reduce total vehicle travel and emissions once the full system is accounted for? Formally, measure the causal net benefit of a microhub including replenishment, handling, empty trips, induced deliveries, and displaced curb activity.
status: Consolidation is a prominent city-logistics strategy, but its benefits depend on system boundaries and utilization, as discussed in Savelsbergh and Van Woensel (2016), *City Logistics: Challenges and Opportunities*.
solved_when: A measurement exists showing whether total vehicle travel and emissions fall after including replenishment, handling, empty trips, induced deliveries, and displaced curb activity.
why: A cleaner last kilometer can conceal a more expensive upstream operation, so claimed benefits may not survive full accounting.
key_works: Savelsbergh and Van Woensel (2016), *City Logistics: Challenges and Opportunities*.

title: Integrated forward and reverse urban logistics
subfield: Freight, urban logistics, and cold chains
open: Can a single operational scheme integrate urban deliveries, returns, reusable packaging flows, and waste collection under uncertain timing, contamination constraints, and mutually incompatible service requirements? In formal terms, this asks for a jointly optimized forward–reverse logistics system that remains robust across organizations and stochastic demand.
status: Reverse and omnichannel logistics have extensive models; robust integration across organizations remains a deployment target. Key work: Savelsbergh and Van Woensel (2016), *City Logistics: Challenges and Opportunities*.
solved_when: A deployable integrated model exists that coordinates deliveries, returns, reusable packaging, and waste collection while explicitly handling uncertain timing, contamination constraints, and incompatible service requirements across organizations.
why: Empty return capacity is valuable only when operational constraints permit reuse; without integration, that value is lost.
key_works: Savelsbergh and Van Woensel (2016), *City Logistics: Challenges and Opportunities*.

title: Where additional truck parking actually helps
subfield: Freight, urban logistics, and cold chains
open: Where and when does adding truck parking actually improve safety and driver productivity, and how large is that causal effect? A formal version asks for estimates of the causal safety and productivity benefit of adding parking at specific places and times, separated from the effect of better information about existing spaces.
status: FMCSA's 2025 research program explicitly targets quantification of parking benefits, and aggregate space counts are known to be insufficient. Key works: FMCSA (2025), *Quantifying the Benefits of Truck Parking*; ATRI (2025), *State-Level Public Truck Parking Findings*.
solved_when: A method exists that quantifies the causal safety and productivity benefits of parking additions at specific places and times, distinct from improvements in information about existing capacity.
why: It directs scarce land and funding toward the shortages that matter most, rather than toward places where added spaces change nothing.
key_works: FMCSA (2025), *Quantifying the Benefits of Truck Parking*; ATRI (2025), *State-Level Public Truck Parking Findings*.

title: Affordable off-grid cold-chain continuity
subfield: Freight, urban logistics, and cold chains
open: Can cold chains be kept unbroken — through outages, loading delays, and transport disruptions — at a cost small producers can actually afford?
status: Sustainable cold-chain technologies already exist, but continuity, financing, and utilization remain jointly limiting, as documented in UNEP and FAO (2022), *Sustainable food cold chains: Opportunities, challenges and the way forward*, DOI:10.4060/cc0923en.
solved_when: Product temperatures are maintained through unreliable electricity, loading delays, and transport disruptions, at costs viable for small producers.
why: A solution prevents food losses without forcing dependence on unaffordable or emissions-intensive infrastructure.
key_works: UNEP and FAO (2022), *Sustainable food cold chains: Opportunities, challenges and the way forward*, DOI:10.4060/cc0923en.

title: Temperature-history-to-quality prediction
subfield: Freight, urban logistics, and cold chains
open: Can the remaining usable quality of a perishable product be predicted from a complete but imperfect temperature history, across varying products, packaging, and microbial conditions? More precisely, can such histories be mapped to a quality estimate robust to the noise and gaps inherent in real cold-chain monitoring?
status: Temperature monitoring is available, but reliable quality inference is more demanding than detecting a threshold violation; no method currently meets that standard. Key works: UNEP and FAO (2022), *Sustainable food cold chains*, DOI:10.4060/cc0923en.
solved_when: A method exists that takes complete, imperfect temperature histories and produces reliable predictions of remaining usable quality that hold across products, packaging types, and microbial conditions — going beyond mere detection of threshold violations.
why: It enables rational routing and disposal decisions rather than blanket rejection of shipments whose temperature records are imperfect.
key_works: UNEP and FAO (2022), *Sustainable food cold chains*, DOI:10.4060/cc0923en.

title: Joint food-loss and refrigeration-emissions optimization
subfield: Freight, urban logistics, and cold chains
open: How should refrigeration levels, routing, and storage policies be chosen so that the combined harms of food loss, energy use, refrigerant leakage, and equipment impacts are minimized across a cold chain? Formally, this asks for jointly optimized policies rather than treating refrigeration energy in isolation.
status: Cold-chain sustainability work, including UNEP and FAO (2022), *Sustainable food cold chains*, DOI:10.4060/cc0923en, identifies interacting burdens and shows that minimizing refrigeration energy alone can increase total harm.
solved_when: A policy (refrigeration, routing, and storage) is given whose combined food-loss, energy, refrigerant, and equipment impacts are minimized, with the optimization framework accounting for the interactions among these burdens.
why: Refrigeration energy is only part of the picture: transport emissions must be weighed against the larger footprint of spoiled products, and minimizing energy alone can increase total harm.
key_works: UNEP and FAO (2022), *Sustainable food cold chains*, DOI:10.4060/cc0923en.

title: Ammonia propulsion with low net climate impact
subfield: Marine propulsion, fuels, and ship environmental performance
open: Does ammonia propulsion deliver genuinely low net climate impact across a full voyage? This requires validating whole-voyage greenhouse performance, accounting for upstream production, nitrous oxide emissions, pilot fuel use, and transient operating conditions.
status: Engines and safety work have advanced; IMO's September 2026 seminar still addresses substantial implementation questions, as recorded in IMO (2026), *Technical Seminar on the use of ammonia as marine fuel*.
solved_when: Whole-voyage greenhouse performance of ammonia propulsion is validated, including quantified contributions from upstream production, nitrous oxide, pilot fuel, and transient operating conditions.
why: Carbon-free fuel molecules do not guarantee low climate impact — slip gases such as nitrous oxide and upstream production pathways can erase the intended climate benefit.
key_works: IMO (2026), *Technical Seminar on the use of ammonia as marine fuel*.

title: Ammonia bunkering risk under realistic failures
subfield: Marine propulsion, fuels, and ship environmental performance
open: Can an integrated safety system — combining detection, containment, evacuation, and emergency response — be shown to work effectively against credible toxic-release scenarios during ammonia bunkering and onboard handling? In formal terms, the goal is a demonstrated, site-specific safety performance covering the full chain from leak detection to response under realistic failure conditions.
status: Guidance and technical development exist, but site-specific integrated safety performance remains to be demonstrated; key reference: IMO (2026), *Technical Seminar on the use of ammonia as marine fuel*.
solved_when: Effective detection, containment, evacuation, and response are demonstrated for credible toxic releases during bunkering and onboard handling at a specific site.
why: Ammonia's toxicity creates risks fundamentally different from those of conventional marine fuels, so without demonstrated integrated safety performance its adoption as a marine fuel cannot proceed responsibly.
key_works: IMO (2026), *Technical Seminar on the use of ammonia as marine fuel*.

title: Transient ammonia-engine emissions maps
subfield: Marine propulsion, fuels, and ship environmental performance
open: What emissions does an ammonia-fueled marine engine actually produce outside steady state — during starts, load changes, prolonged low-load operation, and as after-treatment degrades? A rigorous answer requires measuring and modeling ammonia slip, nitrogen oxides, and nitrous oxide across these transient and rare operating states.
status: Steady operating points are insufficient for voyage-level assessment; transient emissions remain a key validation need. Key works: IMO (2026), *Technical Seminar on the use of ammonia as marine fuel*.
solved_when: A validated dataset and model of ammonia slip, NOx, and N2O covering engine starts, load changes, low-load operation, and after-treatment degradation exist, sufficient to support voyage-level emissions assessment rather than steady-point extrapolation.
why: Rare operating states may dominate important emissions, so steady-state maps cannot be trusted for real voyages; transient data is the missing validation link for ammonia as a marine fuel.
key_works: IMO (2026), *Technical Seminar on the use of ammonia as marine fuel*.

title: Representative real-world methane slip
subfield: Marine propulsion, fuels, and ship environmental performance
open: How much methane do ships actually emit in real-world operation, once age, maintenance, load, weather, and voyage type are taken into account? The goal is to build representative methane-emission factors for ship engines across these varying conditions.
status: The FUMES study (ICCT (2024), *Fugitive and Unburned Methane Emissions from Ships—FUMES*) combined airborne and onboard measurements; representative coverage of the full fleet remains a larger data requirement.
solved_when: Methane-emission factors exist that cover the fleet representatively across engine age, maintenance state, load, weather, and voyage type, rather than only certification-test conditions.
why: Climate comparisons between fuels and technologies are sensitive to operating conditions that certification tests omit, so current assessments can misjudge the climate benefit of methane-fueled ships.
key_works: ICCT (2024), *Fugitive and Unburned Methane Emissions from Ships—FUMES*.

title: Durable low-load methane abatement
subfield: Marine propulsion, fuels, and ship environmental performance
open: Can methane emitted during low-load and transient operation of marine engines be abated durably, without unacceptable fuel penalties, maintenance burden, or loss of effectiveness over time?
status: Real-world measurements identify the importance of operating conditions; durable whole-duty-cycle abatement remains the engineering target. Key work: ICCT (2024), *Fugitive and Unburned Methane Emissions from Ships—FUMES*.
solved_when: An abatement system maintains effectiveness across the whole duty cycle, including low-load and transient conditions, over real-world service, without imposing unacceptable fuel penalties or maintenance burden.
why: Laboratory removal efficiency is insufficient for climate-effective service; only durable whole-duty-cycle abatement translates to real climate benefit.
key_works: ICCT (2024), *Fugitive and Unburned Methane Emissions from Ships—FUMES*.

title: Reconciling ship methane measurements
subfield: Marine propulsion, fuels, and ship environmental performance
open: Can methane emissions from ships be measured in a way that engine tests, observations aboard the vessel, remote sensing of exhaust plumes, and fleet-level inventories all agree on? The task is to bring these methods together within a common uncertainty framework so their results become comparable rather than contradictory.
status: Multiple measurement methods have been deployed, but differing boundaries and sampling create reconciliation challenges. The ICCT (2024) report *Fugitive and Unburned Methane Emissions from Ships—FUMES* is a key work in this area; inverse atmospheric modeling and measurement reconciliation are related approaches.
solved_when: Engine measurements, ship-level observations, remote plume measurements, and fleet inventories can be reconciled within a single common uncertainty framework, with differences in boundaries and sampling accounted for.
why: Without such a framework, incompatible inventories can support contradictory fuel policies; with it, methane emissions data becomes a reliable basis for regulatory and fuel-strategy decisions.
key_works: ICCT (2024), *Fugitive and Unburned Methane Emissions from Ships—FUMES*.

title: Quiet propulsion without efficiency sacrifice
subfield: Marine propulsion, fuels, and ship environmental performance
open: What changes to hull form, propeller design, and operating practice can reduce a vessel's underwater radiated noise across its service conditions while maintaining or even improving energy efficiency? Formally, the task is to identify and experimentally validate design and operational interventions whose noise benefit does not come at an efficiency cost.
status: IMO and MARAD are actively examining the interaction between ship energy efficiency and underwater radiated noise, but co-benefits are not universal: quieting and efficiency do not automatically align. Key works: MARAD (2025), *Vessel Generated Underwater Noise*; IMO (2025), *Workshop on the relationship between ship energy efficiency and underwater radiated noise*.
solved_when: Specific hull, propeller, and operational changes are identified and shown — across service conditions — to reduce underwater radiated noise while maintaining or improving energy efficiency, rather than trading one against the other.
why: It prevents solving one environmental problem (ocean noise) by worsening another (energy use and emissions), and would give regulators and designers concrete co-benefit levers.
key_works: MARAD (2025), *Vessel Generated Underwater Noise*; IMO (2025), *Workshop on the relationship between ship energy efficiency and underwater radiated noise*.

title: Ecologically meaningful ship-noise limits
subfield: Marine propulsion, fuels, and ship environmental performance
open: Can we link the cumulative, frequency-dependent noise exposure from vessels to concrete biological effects across species, habitats, and behavioral contexts? In formal terms, this asks for an exposure–response framework that maps acoustic dose measures onto ecological outcomes rather than decibel levels alone.
status: Noise-reduction guidelines exist — IMO, *Ship noise*, including revised 2023 guidelines and subsequent implementation work — but translating acoustic measures into ecosystem outcomes remains an important evidence gap.
solved_when: A quantitative relationship is established connecting cumulative, frequency-dependent vessel noise exposure to biological effects, validated across species, habitats, and behavioral contexts, so that noise limits can be set in ecological rather than purely acoustic terms.
why: Decibel reductions alone do not establish ecological benefit; without this link, noise-reduction rules cannot be shown to protect marine ecosystems.
key_works: IMO, *Ship noise*, including revised 2023 guidelines and subsequent implementation work.

title: In-water cleaning without biological release
subfield: Marine propulsion, fuels, and ship environmental performance
open: Can ships' hulls be cleaned in the water in a way that reliably captures the removed biofouling organisms and debris, rather than releasing them into the surrounding environment? More formally, the goal is an in-water cleaning method that prevents invasive-species transfer through cleaning discharges while avoiding excessive damage to the hull coating.
status: IMO issued in-water cleaning guidance in 2025 (IMO (2025), *Guidance on in-water cleaning of ships’ biofouling*, MEPC.1/Circ.918); validated performance across conditions remains a deployment requirement.
solved_when: A cleaning approach demonstrates validated capture of organisms and debris, with acceptable coating integrity, across the range of operating conditions required for deployment.
why: Hull cleaning cuts fuel use, but if it releases removed organisms it simply opens a different environmental pathway; solving the capture problem lets the fuel savings be realized without spreading invasive species.
key_works: IMO (2025), *Guidance on in-water cleaning of ships’ biofouling*, MEPC.1/Circ.918.

title: Predictive biofouling maintenance
subfield: Marine propulsion, fuels, and ship environmental performance
open: Can a vessel's biofouling trajectory be predicted well enough from its own operational record — voyage history, idle periods, habitat, fuel penalty, and biological-transfer risk — to choose cleaning or coating interventions automatically rather than by fixed schedule? Formally, the goal is a predictive model and intervention-selection method for individual ships' hull fouling over their lifecycle.
status: Guidelines and management practices exist — notably IMO (2023), *Guidelines for the control and management of ships’ biofouling*, and IMO’s biofouling program — but individualized lifecycle prediction remains the stronger target; no such predictive method is established.
solved_when: A method exists that uses voyage history, idle periods, habitat exposure, fuel penalty, and biological-transfer risk to forecast fouling growth for an individual vessel and select cleaning or coating interventions that outperform fixed cleaning schedules across a fleet with substantial inter-vessel differences.
why: Fixed cleaning schedules miss substantial differences between vessels, so ships are either cleaned too early (wasting cost and dock time) or too late (paying avoidable fuel penalties and raising biological-transfer risk).
key_works: IMO (2023), *Guidelines for the control and management of ships’ biofouling*; IMO’s biofouling program.

title: Truthful just-in-time ship arrivals
subfield: Ports, inland waterways, and maritime networks
open: Can ships be induced to slow-steam en route rather than race to port and wait at anchor? That is, can berth availability, completion times, and readiness information be made reliable enough that a ship is never penalized for arriving later?
status: Just-in-time arrival guidance identifies information and incentive barriers, and notes that technical ETA prediction alone is insufficient. Key work: GEF–UNDP–IMO GloMEEP and GIA (2020), *Just In Time Arrival Guide—Barriers and Potential Solutions*.
solved_when: Berth availability, completion-time, and readiness information is sufficiently reliable that ships can reduce speed without being penalized for arriving later.
why: It eliminates wasteful "sail fast, then wait" behavior, cutting fuel burn and anchorage congestion at ports.
key_works: GEF–UNDP–IMO GloMEEP and GIA (2020), *Just In Time Arrival Guide—Barriers and Potential Solutions*.

title: Robust arrival control under changing berth readiness
subfield: Ports, inland waterways, and maritime networks
open: Can a ship continuously revise its speed and arrival schedule as weather, congestion, and berth completion forecasts evolve over a voyage, while keeping service and fuel penalties within bounded limits? Formally, this asks for an uncertainty-aware arrival-control policy that updates decisions dynamically rather than fixing a single early ETA.
status: Just-in-time arrival concepts and contracts already exist in practice, notably GloMEEP and GIA (2020), *Just In Time Arrival Guide*, and BIMCO (2021), *Just in Time Arrival Clause for Voyage Charter Parties*, but uncertainty-aware operational coordination remains necessary.
solved_when: A control scheme exists that revises speed and arrival decisions in response to changing weather, congestion, and berth readiness forecasts, with provable (or demonstrably bounded) penalties on service delay and fuel consumption.
why: A single early ETA agreement cannot absorb an entire voyage's uncertainty; without dynamic revision, ships face either avoidable fuel burn or missed berth slots.
key_works: GloMEEP and GIA (2020), *Just In Time Arrival Guide*; BIMCO (2021), *Just in Time Arrival Clause for Voyage Charter Parties*.

title: Contractual sharing of arrival-efficiency gains
subfield: Ports, inland waterways, and maritime networks
open: Can enforceable contractual arrangements be designed that align the interests of all parties in a port call — shipowners, charterers, terminals, and cargo owners — so that fuel savings, delay risk, and opportunity costs are shared rather than falling on whichever actor happens to bear them? Formally, the question is what contract structures make it incentive-compatible for each party to participate in and comply with arrival-efficiency improvements.
status: BIMCO (2021), *Just in Time Arrival Clause for Voyage Charter Parties 2021*, provides a contractual mechanism for just-in-time arrivals, but universal alignment across commercial arrangements is not thereby established. Related theoretical framings include incomplete contracts and principal–agent problems.
solved_when: A class of enforceable contractual arrangements exists that distributes fuel savings, delay risk, and opportunity costs among shipowners, charterers, terminals, and cargo owners in a way that achieves alignment across commercial arrangements generally, not only under a particular mechanism.
why: Under current arrangements the actor who pays for an efficiency-improving change often does not receive its benefits, so the gains from arrival coordination go unrealized; well-designed contracts would unlock those savings.
key_works: BIMCO (2021), *Just in Time Arrival Clause for Voyage Charter Parties 2021*.

title: Port electrification without grid bottleneck migration
subfield: Ports, inland waterways, and maritime networks
open: How can a port coordinate shore power, cargo-handling equipment, and truck charging together with grid upgrades, when vessel calls and freight demand are uncertain? Formally, the question is whether a joint investment-and-operation model can schedule these electrified loads and grid expansion so that shared electricity infrastructure does not become the port's new bottleneck.
status: Port decarbonization is advancing, but shared electricity infrastructure creates new coupled constraints; no coordinated solution is yet established. Key background: UNCTAD (2025), *Review of Maritime Transport 2025: Staying the course in turbulent waters*. Related areas include distribution-grid expansion and stochastic energy scheduling.
solved_when: A coordination framework or co-optimization model exists that jointly plans shore power, cargo-handling equipment electrification, truck charging, and grid upgrades under uncertainty in vessel calls and freight demand, and demonstrably avoids coincident-peak overloads of the shared electricity infrastructure.
why: Electrifying each asset separately can create coincident peaks that undermine the whole port; a solution prevents decarbonization from simply migrating the port's bottleneck from fuel to the grid.
key_works: UNCTAD (2025), *Review of Maritime Transport 2025: Staying the course in turbulent waters*.

title: Port asset condition linked to operational consequence
subfield: Ports, inland waterways, and maritime networks
open: Can we build comparable condition and failure-risk data across a port's disparate physical assets — quay walls, cranes, pavements, channels, and utilities — and link that condition to cargo disruption outcomes? In formal terms, the goal is a data-integration framework that translates heterogeneous asset condition measures into operational service risk.
status: Operational performance measures exist, but translating heterogeneous asset condition into service risk remains a data-integration target. Key works: UNCTAD (2025), *Review of Maritime Transport 2025*; Bierwirth and Meisel (2015), *A follow-up survey of berth allocation and quay crane scheduling problems in container terminals*.
solved_when: A framework exists that renders condition and failure-risk data comparable across quay walls, cranes, pavements, channels, and utilities, and links these measures to cargo disruption outcomes.
why: Asset age alone poorly identifies the investments that prevent disruption, so decision-makers lack a defensible basis for prioritizing port maintenance spending.
key_works: UNCTAD (2025), *Review of Maritime Transport 2025*; Bierwirth and Meisel (2015), *A follow-up survey of berth allocation and quay crane scheduling problems in container terminals*.

title: Real-time integrated terminal recovery
subfield: Ports, inland waterways, and maritime networks
open: Can a container terminal jointly reschedule berths, quay cranes, yard operations, and vehicles after a disruption such as an equipment failure or a late vessel arrival, and still produce a provably good recovery plan within the operational deadline?
status: Integrated optimizers and robust formulations exist; large-scale real-time recovery remains a stronger system target. See Bierwirth and Meisel (2015), *A follow-up survey of berth allocation and quay crane scheduling problems in container terminals*, DOI:10.1016/j.ejor.2014.12.030.
solved_when: A recovery method exists that jointly re-optimizes berth, crane, yard, and vehicle schedules with verifiable solution quality (e.g., optimality gaps or bounds) delivered within operational deadlines at large terminal scale.
why: Optimizing one terminal subsystem in isolation can simply push congestion into another, so joint recovery is what actually restores terminal throughput after disruption.
key_works: Bierwirth and Meisel (2015), *A follow-up survey of berth allocation and quay crane scheduling problems in container terminals*, DOI:10.1016/j.ejor.2014.12.030.

title: Drought-aware lock scheduling
subfield: Ports, inland waterways, and maritime networks
open: Can vessels and lock operations on an inland waterway be scheduled jointly when the water itself is a scarce, time-varying resource? Formally, the question is to find schedules that respect water consumption, changing available depth, vessel heterogeneity, and time-sensitive cargo simultaneously.
status: Waterway traffic models are developing, but hydrological constraints make direct transplantation of road-traffic methods inadequate. Key work: Zhuang et al. (2024), *Traffic Flow Theory for Waterway Traffic: Current Challenges and Countermeasures*, DOI:10.3390/jmse12122254.
solved_when: A scheduling method exists that jointly assigns vessels and lockages while explicitly accounting for water consumption, changing available depth, vessel heterogeneity, and time-sensitive cargo, and is shown to outperform throughput-only scheduling on these dimensions.
why: Optimizing throughput alone can consume water that later operations depend on, so without such a method efficiency gains now come at the cost of stranding traffic later.
key_works: Zhuang et al. (2024), *Traffic Flow Theory for Waterway Traffic: Current Challenges and Countermeasures*, DOI:10.3390/jmse12122254.

title: Fundamental diagrams for heterogeneous waterways
subfield: Ports, inland waterways, and maritime networks
open: When do meaningful flow–density relationships exist on waterways shared by vessels of different sizes, maneuverability, drafts, and navigation rules? More formally, characterize the conditions under which a fundamental diagram can be defined for such heterogeneous vessel traffic.
status: A 2024 review identifies difficulties adapting traffic-flow theory to waterways. Key work: Zhuang, Liu, Wang, Guo, and Ni (2024), *Traffic Flow Theory for Waterway Traffic*, DOI:10.3390/jmse12122254.
solved_when: A characterization exists of the conditions under which heterogeneous vessel traffic admits a well-defined flow–density relationship, validated theoretically and/or experimentally.
why: Channel capacity cannot safely be inferred from road analogies alone, so this characterization is needed for sound capacity and safety assessment on inland waterways.
key_works: Zhuang, Liu, Wang, Guo, and Ni (2024), *Traffic Flow Theory for Waterway Traffic*, DOI:10.3390/jmse12122254.

title: Waterway intersection service and safety
subfield: Ports, inland waterways, and maritime networks
open: Can we derive capacity and delay measures for waterway intersections that remain predictive when crossing, overtaking, restricted maneuverability, and collision-avoidance decisions interact?
status: Waterway-specific level-of-service methods exist, notably Liu et al. (2024), *Level of Service Evaluation Method for Waterway Intersections*, DOI:10.3390/jmse12112050; validated generalization across intersection types remains a target.
solved_when: Capacity and delay formulas, or validated estimation methods, are derived and shown to generalize across intersection types under interacting crossing, overtaking, maneuverability, and collision-avoidance behavior.
why: Average traffic volume can conceal dangerous conflict patterns, so aggregates alone can certify a waterway as safe that is not.
key_works: Liu et al. (2024), *Level of Service Evaluation Method for Waterway Intersections*, DOI:10.3390/jmse12112050.

title: Resilient small-island shipping services
subfield: Ports, inland waterways, and maritime networks
open: How can a small-island shipping system — its fleet, subsidies, reserve capacity, and fuel arrangements — be designed so that affordable service survives both chronically low demand and major route disruptions?
status: Maritime assessments, notably UNCTAD (2025), *Review of Maritime Transport 2025: Staying the course in turbulent waters*, document vulnerability and uneven transport costs; durable small-market solutions remain difficult.
solved_when: A concrete, implementable design for fleet, subsidy, reserve-capacity, and fuel strategies is delivered that demonstrably preserves affordable service under low-demand conditions and under major route disruptions.
why: For small islands, shipping disruption can threaten essential supplies rather than merely raise logistics costs.
key_works: UNCTAD (2025), *Review of Maritime Transport 2025: Staying the course in turbulent waters*.

title: Certifiable megawatt-class hybrid-electric propulsion
open: Can a fault-tolerant, maintainable aircraft-wide hybrid-electric propulsion system at megawatt class be demonstrated such that its lifecycle benefits survive the demands of certification and real operations?
status: NASA reported hybrid-electric flight demonstration progress in 2026 through its *Electrified Powertrain Flight Demonstration* program and results, but a first demonstration is not equivalent to fleet-ready integration.
solved_when: A megawatt-class hybrid-electric aircraft-wide propulsion architecture is demonstrated to be fault-tolerant and maintainable, and shown to retain its lifecycle benefits under certification and operational requirements — not merely flown once.
why: It moves electrification from isolated components to useful transport aircraft; without certification-surviving fault tolerance and maintainability, demonstrations do not translate into fleet capability.
key_works: NASA (2026), *Electrified Powertrain Flight Demonstration* program and results.

title: Lightweight high-voltage insulation at altitude
open: Can high-voltage aircraft electrical systems be insulated and protected against partial discharge, arcing, contamination, and aging at altitude without adding so much insulation mass that the propulsion benefit of electrification is lost?
status: Altitude testing has advanced, including NASA's *Electrified Powertrain Flight Demonstration* and NASA–magniX altitude-test reporting, but full-life behavior under combined environmental stresses remains an engineering requirement.
solved_when: An insulation and protection scheme is demonstrated to control partial discharge, arcing, contamination, and aging in high-voltage aircraft systems while keeping insulation and protection mass low enough that propulsion benefits are preserved, with full-life behavior validated under combined environmental stresses.
why: Ground-level electrical performance does not establish safe high-altitude operation; without lightweight insulation that survives the full service life, electrified aircraft propulsion cannot deliver its promised benefit.
key_works: NASA, *Electrified Powertrain Flight Demonstration*; NASA–magniX altitude-test reporting.

title: Aircraft-wide thermal management for electrification
open: Can an aircraft-wide thermal management system reject heat from the motors, power electronics, and energy storage across the full flight envelope without incurring unacceptable penalties in drag, mass, or failure coupling?
status: Electrified powertrain demonstrations have addressed components and integration, but aircraft-level thermal trade-offs remain mission-dependent. Key work: Wen et al. (2023), *Fleet Wide Impacts of the Electrified Powertrain Flight Demonstration Technology Portfolio*, DOI:10.2514/6.2023-3871.
solved_when: A thermal management architecture is demonstrated that handles the combined heat loads of motors, electronics, and storage throughout the flight envelope while keeping drag, mass, and failure-coupling penalties within acceptable bounds.
why: Gains in electrical efficiency can be entirely outweighed by cooling-system penalties, so aircraft-level electrification hinges on solving this.
key_works: Wen et al. (2023), *Fleet Wide Impacts of the Electrified Powertrain Flight Demonstration Technology Portfolio*, DOI:10.2514/6.2023-3871.

title: Distortion-tolerant boundary-layer-ingesting propulsion
open: Can a boundary-layer-ingesting propulsion system hold onto its efficiency, operability, and structural integrity when the fan faces strongly nonuniform inflow across maneuvers and atmospheric disturbances? Formally, this asks for an integrated design that remains stable and fatigue-acceptable under distorted inflow throughout the operating envelope, not just at design point.
status: BLI mechanisms and design approaches are actively studied; robust off-design operation remains a major integration requirement. Hall (2024), *Mechanisms, Benefits, and Challenges of Boundary Layer Ingestion Propulsion*; NASA (2025), *Advancements in Coupled Aeropropulsive Design Optimization*.
solved_when: A BLI configuration demonstrates maintained efficiency, operability, and acceptable fatigue under strongly nonuniform inflow across maneuvers and atmospheric disturbances, including robust off-design operation.
why: Wake-energy recovery is unusable if it produces unacceptable fan instability or fatigue; without distortion tolerance the promised efficiency gains of BLI cannot be realized in service.
key_works: Hall (2024), *Mechanisms, Benefits, and Challenges of Boundary Layer Ingestion Propulsion*; NASA (2025), *Advancements in Coupled Aeropropulsive Design Optimization*.

title: Lightweight hydrogen tanks with aircraft service life
open: Can we design a cryogenic hydrogen storage system that meets aircraft mass, fatigue, crashworthiness, insulation, inspection, and turnaround requirements all at once? Formally, the goal is a tank system satisfying the full combined operational envelope of a commercial aircraft rather than any subset of these constraints.
status: FlyZero developed aircraft concepts and technology roadmaps; satisfying the combined operational envelope remains the target. Key works: Aerospace Technology Institute (2022), *FlyZero: Our Vision for Zero-Carbon Emission Air Travel* and *Advanced Manufacturing*.
solved_when: A cryogenic storage system is demonstrated that simultaneously meets aircraft mass, fatigue, crashworthiness, insulation, inspection, and turnaround requirements — the combined operational envelope as a whole.
why: Hydrogen's mass advantage over conventional fuel is currently consumed by storage volume and the tank-system burden, so without such a tank the fuel's benefit does not translate into a viable aircraft.
key_works: Aerospace Technology Institute (2022), *FlyZero: Our Vision for Zero-Carbon Emission Air Travel* and *Advanced Manufacturing*.

title: Rapid and safe hydrogen-aircraft turnaround
open: Can a hydrogen aircraft be turned around at the gate as quickly and safely as today's jets, covering refueling, venting, leak detection, ground handling, and emergency procedures at service-relevant turnaround times?
status: Hydrogen aircraft concepts require airport integration beyond airborne propulsion feasibility; this turnaround problem remains open. Aerospace Technology Institute (2022), *FlyZero* technology and commercial roadmaps.
solved_when: A demonstration shows refueling, venting, leak detection, ground handling, and emergency procedures all performed at service-relevant turnaround times.
why: An aircraft that cannot be turned around safely and economically is not a viable transport system.
key_works: Aerospace Technology Institute (2022), *FlyZero* technology and commercial roadmaps.

title: Whole-climate comparison of alternative aircraft energy
open: When batteries, hydrogen, and synthetic fuels are compared for aircraft under a single consistent set of boundaries — mission profile, supporting infrastructure, upstream energy supply, and non-CO₂ climate effects — which energy source comes out best for the climate? Formally, the goal is a whole-climate comparison methodology that holds these boundary conditions fixed across the alternatives.
status: Fundamentals-based energy comparisons exist, but their results depend strongly on assumptions and operational context. Key works: Aerospace Technology Institute (2022), *Primary Energy Source Comparison and Selection*, FlyZero.
solved_when: A comparison of batteries, hydrogen, and synthetic fuels is produced under consistent mission, infrastructure, upstream-energy, and non-CO₂ climate boundaries, showing how (or whether) the ranking of the alternatives changes across stated assumptions and operational contexts.
why: Tailpipe carbon accounting alone can rank these technologies incorrectly, so a rigorous whole-climate comparison is needed to guide which alternative aircraft energy deserves development and infrastructure investment.
key_works: Aerospace Technology Institute (2022), *Primary Energy Source Comparison and Selection*, FlyZero.

title: Supercooled-large-droplet icing prediction
open: Can we experimentally validate models of supercooled-large-droplet impingement, splashing, runback, and freezing on aircraft surfaces? In particular, do current models correctly predict where large droplets deposit and freeze water outside the regions covered by conventional icing protection?
status: NASA’s October 5, 2026 report describes new tunnel instrumentation and continuing analysis specifically addressing this gap. Key work: Mann/NASA (2026), *NASA Testing Aims at Supercooled Large Droplet Aviation Safety*.
solved_when: A validated model of large-droplet impingement, splashing, runback, and freezing accurately predicts water deposition outside conventional protected regions, confirmed against experimental data from the new tunnel instrumentation.
why: Existing icing protection can miss where large droplets deposit water, leaving aircraft vulnerable to ice accretion outside protected areas.
key_works: Mann/NASA (2026), *NASA Testing Aims at Supercooled Large Droplet Aviation Safety*.

title: Community response to repeated low-boom flight
open: What level of exposure to repeated shaped sonic booms do communities actually find acceptable, across different buildings, activities, populations, and atmospheric conditions? In other words, can a defensible exposure criterion be established from community response data gathered under realistic, repeated low-boom flight operations?
status: X-59 flight testing has advanced in 2026, but flight capability alone does not establish community acceptability. Key works: NASA (2026), *NASA’s X-59 Aircraft Flies Supersonic for First Time* and continuing Quesst flight-test reporting.
solved_when: A community-acceptability criterion for repeated shaped sonic booms is established, quantifying acceptable exposure across the varying buildings, activities, populations, and atmospheric conditions considered.
why: Low-boom transport requires social and acoustic evidence beyond a single overflight; without demonstrated community acceptability, flight capability alone cannot justify overland supersonic operations.
key_works: NASA (2026), *NASA’s X-59 Aircraft Flies Supersonic for First Time* and continuing Quesst flight-test reporting.

title: Humidity forecasts for contrail decisions
subfield: Air traffic, contrails, drones, and advanced air mobility
open: Can ice-supersaturated regions in the atmosphere be forecast with enough accuracy that rerouting flights to avoid contrails still yields a net climate benefit once forecast uncertainty is accounted for? Formally, the question is whether prediction of these regions can be made accurate enough that the expected contrail energy forcing avoided exceeds the fuel penalty of the reroute under uncertainty.
status: Contrail-energy predictions are known to be sensitive to humidity and model parameters, and uncertainty-aware prediction remains a central open issue in this area; Platt et al. (2024), *The effect of uncertainty in humidity and model parameters on the prediction of contrail energy forcing*, examines this sensitivity directly.
solved_when: A humidity-forecast-driven rerouting strategy demonstrably remains beneficial — i.e., the climate benefit of avoided contrail energy forcing outweighs the added fuel burn — after uncertainty in humidity and model parameters is fully included in the prediction.
why: Incorrect avoidance forecasts waste fuel without preventing warming, so forecasts that cannot handle their own uncertainty can make contrail mitigation actively counterproductive.
key_works: Platt et al. (2024), *The effect of uncertainty in humidity and model parameters on the prediction of contrail energy forcing*.

title: Satellite detection bias in contrail evaluation
subfield: Air traffic, contrails, drones, and advanced air mobility
open: How many contrails do satellite observations miss or misclassify, and how can evaluation metrics be corrected for this selection effect? Formally, the goal is to quantify the detection bias in satellite-based contrail observation and build corrected performance metrics that account for it.
status: A 2025 study, Driver et al. (2025), *Factors limiting contrail detection in satellite imagery*, DOI:10.5194/amt-18-1115-2025, identifies factors limiting detection and notes that observed contrails are not a complete census.
solved_when: The factors limiting contrail detection in satellite imagery are quantified, and contrail evaluation metrics are corrected so that observed outcomes no longer serve as an incomplete census of true contrail formation.
why: Avoidance trials can appear successful merely because their outcomes become harder to observe; corrected metrics prevent false conclusions about mitigation effectiveness.
key_works: Driver et al. (2025), *Factors limiting contrail detection in satellite imagery*, DOI:10.5194/amt-18-1115-2025.

title: Causal climate benefit of contrail avoidance
subfield: Air traffic, contrails, drones, and advanced air mobility
open: Does operational contrail avoidance actually change Earth's radiation budget, when measured directly rather than inferred from models? In formal terms, can we causally attribute a change in realized climate forcing to avoidance decisions, rather than relying on predicted contrail occurrence or estimated energy forcing?
status: A 2026 Asia-Pacific trial reported promising estimated effects, but modeled impact is not direct measurement of realized forcing. Key works: Armada and Vogler (2026), *Our new contrail avoidance trial in Asia-Pacific*; Bräuer et al. (2021), DOI:10.1029/2020GL092166.
solved_when: A controlled or quasi-experimental field measurement demonstrates a causal change in realized climate forcing attributable to avoidance operations, distinct from modeled contrail occurrence or estimated energy forcing.
why: It establishes whether operational changes airlines actually make deliver the intended climate benefit; without direct causal evidence, avoidance efforts may optimize a proxy rather than the climate outcome itself.
key_works: Armada and Vogler (2026), *Our new contrail avoidance trial in Asia-Pacific*; Bräuer et al. (2021), DOI:10.1029/2020GL092166.

title: Joint fuel–contrail dispatch optimization
subfield: Air traffic, contrails, drones, and advanced air mobility
open: When a flight alters its route to avoid forming a contrail, how should avoidance actions be chosen robustly when the extra fuel emissions, contrail forcing, airspace constraints, and forecast errors all interact?
status: Avoidance trials and uncertainty studies provide components; dependable whole-network optimization remains the stronger target. Key works: Platt et al. (2024), *The effect of uncertainty…*; Armada and Vogler (2026), *Our new contrail avoidance trial in Asia-Pacific*.
solved_when: A dependable whole-network optimization method exists that selects avoidance actions accounting jointly for fuel emissions, contrail forcing, airspace constraints, and forecast uncertainty — beyond the current component-level trials and uncertainty studies.
why: Preventing one contrail can increase another flight's fuel use or delay, so without a joint framework the climate benefit of avoidance can be offset or reversed elsewhere in the network.
key_works: Platt et al. (2024), *The effect of uncertainty…*; Armada and Vogler (2026), *Our new contrail avoidance trial in Asia-Pacific*.

title: Multi-operator low-altitude deconfliction
subfield: Air traffic, contrails, drones, and advanced air mobility
open: How can independently operated drone fleets, each with only partial information about the others, coordinate low-altitude operations so that separation is guaranteed and the system recovers safely when plans turn out inconsistent or a service fails?
status: NASA's High Density Vertiplex work integrates prototype systems and conducts multivehicle flight tests (Schaefer et al. (2024), *High Density Vertiplex—Scalable Autonomous Operations—Flight Test Report*, NASA NTRS 20240007438); broad interoperable operation remains a larger requirement.
solved_when: A demonstrated coordination mechanism exists that maintains separation guarantees across independent operators under incomplete information and tolerates inconsistent plans or failed services, validated through integrated multivehicle flight testing.
why: Each operator's individually safe plan can conflict with another operator's plan, so without such coordination, combining independently validated fleets does not yield a jointly safe system.
key_works: Schaefer et al. (2024), *High Density Vertiplex—Scalable Autonomous Operations—Flight Test Report*, NASA NTRS 20240007438.

title: Missed approaches in dense vertiport networks
subfield: Air traffic, contrails, drones, and advanced air mobility
open: How can a dense vertiport network preserve safe escape and diversion options when multiple arrivals must execute missed approaches at once, as happens under correlated weather or infrastructure failures?
status: NASA has explored missed-approach concepts (NASA (2023), *Missed Approach Procedures in Advanced Air Mobility: Conceptual Exploration*, NTRS 20230007215); dense interacting operations still require broader validation.
solved_when: Procedures exist that maintain protected recovery capacity for several simultaneous missed approaches under correlated failure conditions, validated experimentally for dense interacting operations.
why: Nominal arrival capacity figures are misleading unless a protected recovery capacity for missed approaches is guaranteed; without it, dense operations could become unsafe precisely when disruptions correlate.
key_works: NASA (2023), *Missed Approach Procedures in Advanced Air Mobility: Conceptual Exploration*, NTRS 20230007215.

title: Human supervision limits for aircraft fleets
subfield: Air traffic, contrails, drones, and advanced air mobility
open: How many aircraft can a single human operator safely supervise, and how does that ratio change with the reliability of the automation, the correlation among alerts, task complexity, and operator fatigue?
status: Human–autonomy teaming research identifies the challenge, but a fixed vehicles-per-operator number cannot cover all conditions; see Holbrook et al. (2020), *Enabling Urban Air Mobility: Human-Autonomy Teaming Research Challenges and Recommendations*, NTRS 20205002387.
solved_when: A validated determination of safe supervision ratios is obtained as a function of automation reliability, alert correlation, task complexity, and operator fatigue.
why: Labor savings from fleet automation depend on avoiding operator overload during exceptional events.
key_works: Holbrook et al. (2020), *Enabling Urban Air Mobility: Human-Autonomy Teaming Research Challenges and Recommendations*, NTRS 20205002387.

title: Safe handover during simultaneous aircraft emergencies
subfield: Air traffic, contrails, drones, and advanced air mobility
open: When several aircraft demand intervention at the same time, how should a supervising human or automation system allocate attention and hand over authority across them? A satisfactory answer must give explicit guarantees for the vehicles that are left temporarily unattended.
status: Human–autonomy research recognizes teaming and responsibility issues, as in Holbrook et al. (2020), *Enabling Urban Air Mobility: Human-Autonomy Teaming Research Challenges and Recommendations*, but correlated emergencies remain a stronger stress case than the isolated alerts typically studied.
solved_when: A handover and attention-allocation scheme is demonstrated (in experiment or engineering prototype) that handles multiple simultaneous aircraft emergencies while providing explicit, checkable guarantees on the safety of unattended vehicles.
why: Rare common-cause events can defeat otherwise efficient fleet supervision; without such a scheme, a single correlated emergency can cascade across an otherwise well-managed fleet.
key_works: Holbrook et al. (2020), *Enabling Urban Air Mobility: Human-Autonomy Teaming Research Challenges and Recommendations*.

title: Vertiport slots coupled to charging and reserves
subfield: Air traffic, contrails, drones, and advanced air mobility
open: Can vertiport operations be scheduled so that pad slots, charging, passenger turnaround, and diversion reserves are planned jointly rather than sequentially, when energy availability and turnaround times are uncertain? Formally, this asks for a scheduling model that couples slot allocation with aircraft energy state and reserve requirements under stochastic timing and energy deviations.
status: Integrated vertiport prototypes exist, but small-aircraft surrogate tests do not close every full-scale capacity constraint. Key work: Schaefer et al. (2024), *High Density Vertiplex—Scalable Autonomous Operations—Flight Test Report*.
solved_when: A scheduling approach exists that jointly allocates arrival/departure slots, charging resources, passenger handling, and diversion reserves under uncertain energy and turnaround times, and is validated against full-scale vertiport capacity constraints — closing every such constraint that current small-aircraft surrogate tests leave open.
why: Without joint coupling, a landing pad can be available while the aircraft's onward operation is infeasible — pad-level scheduling alone does not guarantee flyable downstream operations.
key_works: Schaefer et al. (2024), *High Density Vertiplex—Scalable Autonomous Operations—Flight Test Report*.

title: Fleet-interface usability under operational stress
subfield: Air traffic, contrails, drones, and advanced air mobility
open: Do fleet-management interfaces for high-density air mobility operations remain usable when operators face long shifts, unfamiliar failure modes, high alert rates, and diverse experience levels? A validation is needed that goes beyond laboratory usability to establish resilient operational performance under realistic stress.
status: NASA (2022) has evaluated fleet-management interfaces in *Usability Evaluation of Fleet Management Interface for High Density Vertiplex Environments* (NTRS 20220009874), but laboratory usability does not establish resilient operational performance.
solved_when: Interfaces are validated — through experimental evaluation — as remaining usable across long shifts, unfamiliar failures, high alert rates, and diverse operator experience, demonstrating resilient operational performance rather than only laboratory usability.
why: Automation can shift rather than remove workload, so interfaces that look usable in the lab may fail operationally under stress.
key_works: NASA (2022), *Usability Evaluation of Fleet Management Interface for High Density Vertiplex Environments*, NTRS 20220009874.

title: Explaining divergent road-fatality trends
open: Why have road-fatality rates moved in such different directions across populations? A satisfactory answer would separate the contributions of exposure, speed, vehicle mix, infrastructure, behavior, reporting, and emergency care to changing fatality rates.
status: Global monitoring documents large differences in fatality trends across populations, but aggregate trends do not identify the best causal intervention.
solved_when: A decomposition exists that attributes observed changes in fatality rates across populations to the listed factors — exposure, speed, vehicle mix, infrastructure, behavior, reporting, and emergency care — in a way that identifies which causal intervention would most reduce fatalities.
