why: Different causes require different countermeasures; without knowing which factor drives a given trend, safety policy cannot target the intervention that actually works.
key_works: WHO (2023), *Global status report on road safety 2023*.

title: Comparable serious-injury surveillance
open: Can police, hospital, emergency-service, and mortality records be linked so that serious road injuries are estimated consistently across sources, with underreporting explicitly corrected? In formal terms, this asks for a surveillance framework that reconciles these datasets into a single comparable measure of serious injury.
status: Fatalities receive more consistent attention than nonfatal outcomes; comparable injury surveillance remains an important gap. The reference point is WHO (2023), *Global status report on road safety 2023*; related approaches include privacy-preserving record linkage and capture–recapture estimation.
solved_when: A method exists that links police, hospital, emergency-service, and mortality records and yields consistent estimates of serious injuries with documented correction of underreporting.
why: Fatality-only metrics miss a large burden of lifelong disability, so without comparable injury surveillance the true scale of nonfatal harm stays invisible to policy.
key_works: WHO (2023), *Global status report on road safety 2023*.

title: Cost-effective post-crash care expansion
open: Which combinations of dispatch, first response, transport, and trauma capability most reduce preventable death after road crashes in underserved regions? Formally, this asks for allocation evidence across the post-crash care chain that is transferable across local settings.
status: Post-crash response is part of established road-safety strategy; locally transferable allocation evidence remains necessary. WHO (2023), *Global status report on road safety 2023*.
solved_when: Specific combinations of dispatch, first response, transport, and trauma capability are identified, with evidence of their effect on preventable death that is locally transferable to underserved regions.
why: Similar crashes can have very different outcomes depending on access to care, so better allocation evidence directly determines who survives.
key_works: WHO (2023), *Global status report on road safety 2023*.

title: Network effects of crossing retrofits
open: Does a crossing improvement reduce total injury risk once pedestrians and drivers reroute, rather than only at the treated crossing itself? Formally, can an experimental or quasi-experimental design capture network-level treatment effects under spatial interference between treated and untreated sites?
status: Individual countermeasures have evidence, including FHWA's *Pedestrian Hybrid Beacons* under Proven Safety Countermeasures; network spillovers and route substitution require additional evaluation. Related work connects the problem to causal inference with spatial interference.
solved_when: A study measures injury risk across the network after a crossing retrofit, capturing rerouting and spillover effects, and shows whether total risk falls, rises, or is unchanged relative to the counterfactual — not merely that risk at the treated crossing decreased.
why: Local safety gains may be offset or amplified elsewhere, so planners could be misjudging countermeasures that appear effective at the site level.
key_works: FHWA, *Pedestrian Hybrid Beacons*, Proven Safety Countermeasures.

title: Safety retrofit portfolios under fixed budgets
open: Given a fixed safety budget, which combination of proven road-safety treatments should be deployed across a network to achieve the greatest reduction in serious injuries — once uncertainty, interactions between treatments, and distributional constraints are properly accounted for?
status: Treatment evidence does not uniquely determine the best network-wide portfolio. Related lines of work include stochastic knapsack optimization and equitable resource allocation; proven countermeasures are catalogued by FHWA in *Proven Safety Countermeasures*, including *Pedestrian Hybrid Beacons*.
solved_when: A method exists that selects a portfolio of proven treatments under a fixed budget while explicitly handling uncertainty in treatment effects, interactions among treatments, and distributional (equity) constraints, and demonstrably outperforms treatment-by-treatment selection on serious-injury reduction.
why: How the budget is allocated across a network matters as much as identifying effective individual devices; a poor allocation wastes the benefit of treatments known to work.
key_works: FHWA, *Proven Safety Countermeasures*, including *Pedestrian Hybrid Beacons*.

title: Causal sources of unequal road trauma
open: How much of the disproportionate road-injury burden carried by some groups is caused by infrastructure, exposure, vehicle access, enforcement, and post-crash care, rather than by individual behavior? Formally, the goal is to decompose and quantify the causal contribution of these structural factors to observed inequities in injury outcomes.
status: Transportation inequities are documented, but explanatory and intervention-ready metrics remain incomplete. Key work: National Academies (2024), *Critical Issues in Transportation for 2024 and Beyond*, "Promoting Equity and Inclusion." Related approaches include social epidemiology and mediation analysis.
solved_when: A validated decomposition exists that quantifies the causal share of infrastructure, exposure, vehicle access, enforcement, and care in unequal road trauma, without residual attribution to individual behavior, and yields intervention-ready metrics.
why: It converts documented disparities into actionable levers, letting policymakers design interventions that attack causes rather than merely re-describe who is being hurt.
key_works: National Academies (2024), *Critical Issues in Transportation for 2024 and Beyond*, “Promoting Equity and Inclusion.”

title: Long-term adaptation to driver assistance
open: How does sustained use of driver-assistance systems reshape attention, skill, trust, and risk-taking over time, and do the safety benefits seen early on persist? Formally, what longitudinal changes in driver behavior and capacity emerge with prolonged assistance, and which of the initial gains survive adaptation?
status: Transition experiments establish substantial human variability, and longitudinal adaptation is known to require longer observation than one-session studies provide. Key work: Eriksson and Stanton (2017), *Takeover Time in Highly Automated Vehicles: Noncritical Transitions to and From Manual Control*, DOI:10.1177/0018720816685832.
solved_when: Longitudinal measurements of attention, skill, trust, and risk-taking are collected over sustained use (longer than one-session observation windows), showing whether initial safety benefits persist or erode.
why: Drivers can adapt to automation in ways that alter its eventual effect, so the safety case for assistance systems depends on their long-term, not just initial, impact.
key_works: Eriksson and Stanton (2017), *Takeover Time in Highly Automated Vehicles: Noncritical Transitions to and From Manual Control*, DOI:10.1177/0018720816685832.

title: Tail-safe takeover timing
open: How should a vehicle schedule the takeover request when control passes back to a human driver who may respond slowly? The goal is a design policy for takeover timing that accounts for the slow, unreliable tails of human response, including task engagement, impairment, and situation complexity.
status: Experimental takeover times vary widely, and designing around a mean or median has been shown to be inadequate. Eriksson and Stanton (2017), *Takeover Time in Highly Automated Vehicles*, DOI:10.1177/0018720816685832.
solved_when: A takeover policy is specified that, rather than optimizing around a mean or median response time, explicitly handles the wide variability of experimentally observed takeover times and remains safe across the tail of the response-time distribution.
why: Safety-critical transitions from automation to human control are determined by tail behavior, so designs built on average response times can fail exactly when it matters.
key_works: Eriksson and Stanton (2017), *Takeover Time in Highly Automated Vehicles*, DOI:10.1177/0018720816685832.

title: Pedestrian-safe large-vehicle geometry
open: Can large-vehicle front-end geometries be designed that meaningfully reduce pedestrian injury risk across a range of pedestrian statures and impact speeds, while still meeting visibility, cooling, crashworthiness, and utility requirements?
status: Real-world studies associate taller, blunter front ends with greater fatality risk; integrated redesign remains the engineering target. Key work: IIHS (2023), *Vehicles with higher, more vertical front ends pose greater risk to pedestrians*.
solved_when: A feasible front-end design (or family of designs) is identified that demonstrably reduces pedestrian harm across stature and impact speed without violating visibility, cooling, crashworthiness, and utility constraints.
why: Collision-avoidance technology cannot prevent every collision, so passive geometric protection remains essential for pedestrians struck by large vehicles.
key_works: IIHS (2023), *Vehicles with higher, more vertical front ends pose greater risk to pedestrians*.

title: Representative pedestrian-impact evaluation
open: Can we build pedestrian-impact test populations and injury models that represent children, older adults, people of different body sizes, and mobility-device users, instead of evaluating safety against a single narrow surrogate? More formally, the goal is a validated experimental and data framework whose coverage spans these population groups.
status: Geometry–fatality associations motivate broader evaluation — IIHS (2023), *Vehicles with higher, more vertical front ends pose greater risk to pedestrians* — but population coverage remains a distinct evidence requirement.
solved_when: Test populations and corresponding injury models exist that cover children, older adults, different body sizes, and mobility-device users, and are used in place of a narrow surrogate in pedestrian-impact evaluation.
why: A vehicle design optimized for one test body may protect other populations poorly, so representative evaluation is needed to make safety claims valid across the real pedestrian population.
key_works: IIHS (2023), *Vehicles with higher, more vertical front ends pose greater risk to pedestrians*.

title: Statistically defensible rare-event safety assurance
open: How can evidence from simulation, targeted testing, operational data, and formal arguments be fused into statistically calibrated estimates of rare severe autonomous-vehicle failures? A complete answer would yield confidence bounds on failure rates that remain valid across heterogeneous evidence sources rather than relying on unvalidated extrapolation.
status: Conventional mileage accumulation can require impractically large exposure; alternative evidence must avoid unvalidated extrapolation. Kalra and Paddock (2016), *Driving to Safety: How Many Miles of Driving Would It Take to Demonstrate Autonomous Vehicle Reliability?*, RAND RR-1478, quantify the exposure burden.
solved_when: A method exists that combines these evidence sources and produces calibrated rare-event failure-rate estimates with quantified uncertainty, without requiring the impractical exposure levels of pure mileage accumulation and without unvalidated extrapolation.
why: It makes safety claims testable without waiting for enormous numbers of crashes, replacing billions of miles of demonstration driving with defensible statistical evidence.
key_works: Kalra and Paddock (2016), *Driving to Safety: How Many Miles of Driving Would It Take to Demonstrate Autonomous Vehicle Reliability?*, RAND RR-1478.

title: Simulation-to-road risk calibration
open: How do errors in a driving simulator propagate into the estimated collision risk of a controller, and under what conditions can an improvement demonstrated in simulation be trusted to carry over to real-world operation? Formally, this asks for a calibration (or bound) relating simulator fidelity to the gap between simulated and operational risk.
status: Open driving simulators enable extensive testing, but visual realism does not establish risk fidelity; the propagation of simulator error into collision-risk estimates remains unquantified. A key enabling tool is Dosovitskiy et al. (2017), *CARLA: An Open Urban Driving Simulator*, arXiv:1711.03938.
solved_when: A quantitative account exists that maps simulator error to change in estimated collision risk, together with a criterion identifying when simulated improvements predict real operational improvements.
why: Without such calibration, a controller can exploit simulator weaknesses and appear safer in testing without actually becoming safer on the road.
key_works: Dosovitskiy et al. (2017), *CARLA: An Open Urban Driving Simulator*, arXiv:1711.03938.

title: Counterfactual realism of simulated road users
open: How should other drivers and pedestrians be modeled to respond when an autonomous vehicle takes actions unlike those in the recorded data? More formally, the question is how to construct simulated road users whose counterfactual behavior is faithful, given that logged trajectories only partially constrain it.
status: Data-driven interactive simulators have advanced, notably Waymax (Gulino et al. (2023), *Waymax: An Accelerated, Data-Driven Simulator for Large-Scale Autonomous Driving Research*, arXiv:2310.08710), but counterfactual behavior is only partially constrained by logged trajectories, so the problem remains open.
solved_when: A simulator of interactive road users exists whose counterfactual responses to off-distribution autonomous-vehicle actions are demonstrably faithful, validated experimentally against real interactive behavior rather than replay alone.
why: Replay-based testing cannot reveal every interactive failure; without valid counterfactual models, off-nominal autonomy actions cannot be safety-tested credibly.
key_works: Gulino et al. (2023), *Waymax: An Accelerated, Data-Driven Simulator for Large-Scale Autonomous Driving Research*, arXiv:2310.08710.

title: Formal safety with uncertain perception
open: How can the uncertainty inherent in perception be incorporated into formal guarantees of driving safety, without either assuming perfectly known object states or falling back on unreasonably conservative behavior?
status: Formal driving models specify safety rules under assumptions, and integrating calibrated perception uncertainty into them remains a broader open challenge. The key work here is Shalev-Shwartz, Shammah, and Shashua (2017), *On a Formal Model of Safe and Scalable Self-driving Cars*, arXiv:1708.06374.
solved_when: A framework is established that formally connects calibrated perception uncertainty to driving-model safety guarantees, yielding provable safety under uncertain object states with behavior that remains reasonable rather than excessively conservative.
why: A correct planner cannot compensate for an unrecognized hazard unless uncertainty is represented; without this link, formal safety claims silently fail whenever perception is imperfect.
key_works: Shalev-Shwartz, Shammah, and Shashua (2017), *On a Formal Model of Safe and Scalable Self-driving Cars*, arXiv:1708.06374.

title: Safe driving without interaction deadlock
open: Can an autonomous vehicle be guaranteed to make meaningful progress through ambiguous interactions with other road users — merging, negotiating right-of-way — without either compromising safety or assuming that others always cooperate? Formally, the challenge is to establish liveness guarantees for driving policies under social interaction uncertainty, alongside the usual safety guarantees.
status: Formal safety frameworks address collision responsibility — notably Shalev-Shwartz, Shammah, and Shashua (2017), *On a Formal Model of Safe and Scalable Self-driving Cars* — but liveness under uncertain social interaction remains a separate requirement that these frameworks do not cover.
solved_when: A driving policy and its analysis exist that jointly guarantee safety and liveness — no collisions under the chosen responsibility-based safety model, and eventual useful progress through ambiguous negotiations — without assuming cooperative behavior from other road users.
why: A vehicle that never crashes because it never proceeds is not useful transportation; without a liveness guarantee, safety-certified vehicles risk interaction deadlock, rendering them operationally useless despite being provably safe.
key_works: Shalev-Shwartz, Shammah, and Shashua (2017), *On a Formal Model of Safe and Scalable Self-driving Cars*.

title: Sensor fusion under asymmetric weather degradation
open: Can a sensor-fusion system keep its object-detection accuracy well calibrated when fog, rain, spray, glare, or contamination degrade different sensors at different rates and in combinations never seen during development? Formally, the goal is a fusion pipeline whose reported confidences remain reliable under asymmetric, previously unseen weather degradation across modalities.
status: Adverse-weather datasets and adaptive fusion methods have improved robustness, but coverage of rare combinations of degradation remains incomplete. Key work: Bijelic et al. (2020), *Seeing Through Fog Without Seeing Fog: Deep Multimodal Sensor Fusion in Unseen Adverse Weather*, arXiv:1902.08913.
solved_when: Object detection remains calibrated across degraded and previously unseen sensor-degradation combinations, with confidence tracking each sensor's changing reliability rather than silently misweighting degraded inputs.
why: Sensor redundancy fails precisely when reported confidence does not track which sensors are currently reliable; without this, an assurance case for autonomous driving in adverse weather collapses.
key_works: Bijelic et al. (2020), *Seeing Through Fog Without Seeing Fog: Deep Multimodal Sensor Fusion in Unseen Adverse Weather*, arXiv:1902.08913.

title: Ground truth for extreme-weather driving
open: How can we obtain trustworthy ground-truth labels for objects, visibility, friction, and sensor state in extreme-weather driving, when the very sensors that would ordinarily provide those labels are themselves degraded by the conditions?
status: Large adverse-weather datasets exist, but severe conditions are rare and difficult to annotate reliably. Key work: Bijelic et al. (2020), *Seeing Through Fog Without Seeing Fog*, arXiv:1902.08913.
solved_when: A dataset and labeling pipeline exists that delivers reliable object, visibility, friction, and sensor-state labels under severe adverse-weather conditions, suitable as a benchmark reference.
why: A benchmark cannot validate robustness when its reference labels are unreliable; without trustworthy ground truth, claims of extreme-weather driving safety cannot be verified.
key_works: Bijelic et al. (2020), *Seeing Through Fog Without Seeing Fog*, arXiv:1902.08913.

title: Reliable operational-domain boundary detection
open: Can a self-driving system recognize, while driving, that it is leaving the operating domain within which it was validated — early enough to reach a safe state, even when the departure is gradual or the result of interacting changes? Formally, this asks for reliable online detection of the boundary of the validated operational domain under non-abrupt, coupled condition shifts.
status: Defined operating domains and test environments already exist, but reliable online recognition of domain boundaries is a stronger operational requirement that remains unmet. Key works: Kalra and Paddock (2016), *Driving to Safety*; Dosovitskiy et al. (2017), *CARLA*.
solved_when: An online detector exists that flags departure from the validated operating domain — including gradual and interacting changes — with enough lead time for the vehicle to transition to a safe state.
why: All safety evidence for an autonomous vehicle is conditional on its assumptions holding, so without knowing when those assumptions stop applying the evidence silently becomes invalid.
key_works: Kalra and Paddock (2016), *Driving to Safety*; Dosovitskiy et al. (2017), *CARLA*.

title: Autonomous service recovery beyond nominal driving
open: Can an autonomous mobility service complete, or safely terminate, journeys when things go wrong — a blocked pickup point, an unreachable drop-off, a vehicle fault, or loss of communication — without silent reliance on undocumented human intervention? Formally, the goal is a recovery capability and supporting evidence base that extends beyond nominal driving to full end-to-end service completion.
status: Current driving benchmarks emphasize motion planning — e.g., Caesar et al. (2021), *nuPlan*, and Gulino et al. (2023), *Waymax* — whereas end-to-end service recovery requires additional tasks and evidence that these benchmarks do not provide.
solved_when: A system demonstrates completion or safe resolution of journeys under blocked pickup locations, inaccessible drop-offs, vehicle faults, and communication loss, without undocumented human rescue, together with tasks and evidence covering these service-recovery scenarios beyond existing motion-planning benchmarks.
why: Successful driving segments do not guarantee completed transportation; without recovery capability, the service fails precisely when it matters operationally.
key_works: Caesar et al. (2021), *nuPlan*; Gulino et al. (2023), *Waymax*.

title: Tenfold fewer failed public charging sessions
open: Can engineering practice reduce failed public charging sessions tenfold against a matched baseline, counting failures across the whole session — payment, authentication, connection, power delivery, and completion?
status: A published field study (Rempel et al. (2024), *Reliability of Open Public Electric Vehicle Direct Current Fast Chargers*, DOI:10.1177/00187208231215242) found only 73.3% of 655 tested ports functional, and noted that reported uptime is not identical to successful charging.
solved_when: A demonstrated system achieves a tenfold reduction in failed charging sessions relative to a matched baseline, with failures measured end-to-end (payment, authentication, connection, power delivery, and completion).
why: Reliability directly affects practical vehicle usability; a driver who cannot depend on a public charger functioning cannot depend on an electric vehicle for everyday transport.
key_works: Rempel et al. (2024), *Reliability of Open Public Electric Vehicle Direct Current Fast Chargers*, DOI:10.1177/00187208231215242.

title: Physically accessible charging across vehicle designs
open: Can electric-vehicle charging be made physically accessible across the full range of inlet locations, cable weights, vehicle dimensions, and user mobility limitations, without requiring unsafe parking or assistance from others?
status: Field reliability work identifies physical usability failures as well as electronic faults. Key work: Rempel et al. (2024), *Reliability of Open Public Electric Vehicle Direct Current Fast Chargers*.
solved_when: A charging design or approach is demonstrated that users with varied mobility limitations, vehicle types, and inlet placements can operate safely and independently, with no need for unsafe parking maneuvers or third-party assistance.
why: An energized charger can still be physically unusable, so reliability alone does not guarantee a working charging experience.
key_works: Rempel et al. (2024), *Reliability of Open Public Electric Vehicle Direct Current Fast Chargers*.

title: Megawatt charging without excessive grid delay
open: Can heavy-duty charging be deployed at freight-relevant locations fast enough that trucks never wait on the grid — coordinating interconnection, storage, power sharing, and uncertain demand growth? Formally: what local power-system designs let megawatt-scale charging be staged in as the freight corridor network rolls out?
status: The 2024 National Zero-Emission Freight Corridor Strategy, from the Joint Office and partner agencies (2024), provides a phased framework for corridor buildout; executing it requires local power-system solutions.
solved_when: Charging infrastructure at freight-relevant locations is deployed in step with truck deployment, with local power-system solutions in place for interconnection coordination, storage, power sharing, and demand-growth uncertainty under the phased framework of the 2024 National Zero-Emission Freight Corridor Strategy.
why: Truck deployment can outpace usable charging infrastructure, leaving vehicles without adequate charging at the locations freight actually uses.
key_works: Joint Office and partner agencies (2024), *National Zero-Emission Freight Corridor Strategy*.

title: Heavy-duty charging schedules compatible with battery life
open: Can we design charging schedules for heavy-duty electric freight vehicles that jointly optimize charging rate, battery temperature, delivery schedule, and payload while explicitly accounting for long-term battery degradation over real freight duty cycles?
status: Corridor planning and electrification studies — including the *National Zero-Emission Freight Corridor Strategy* (2024) and ACEEE (2026), *Advancing Zero-Emission Freight Corridors* — establish the need; the open gap is that useful optimization must include long-term asset effects.
solved_when: A schedule optimization method demonstrably balances charging rate, temperature, delivery timing, and payload on real freight duty cycles, with battery degradation modeled as a long-term asset effect in the objective.
why: Fast charging can trade today's productivity against tomorrow's battery availability, so without degradation-aware scheduling fleets risk systematically shortening battery life.
key_works: *National Zero-Emission Freight Corridor Strategy* (2024); ACEEE (2026), *Advancing Zero-Emission Freight Corridors*.

title: Financing initially underused freight charging
open: How can investment in freight charging infrastructure and risk-sharing among public and private actors be structured so that essential corridors open before utilization is high, without locking in assets that remain uneconomic indefinitely?
status: National strategies already recognize phased deployment — see Joint Office and partner agencies (2024), *National Zero-Emission Freight Corridor Strategy* — but the adoption–infrastructure coordination problem remains site-specific.
solved_when: A funding and staging structure is specified under which charging capacity on essential corridors is deployed ahead of demand, with risk-sharing arrangements that avoid persistent lock-in of uneconomic assets — evaluated against site-specific corridor conditions.
why: Waiting for demand and waiting for infrastructure can reinforce one another, so corridors risk never opening at all; breaking this coordination failure is what the financing structure must achieve.
key_works: Joint Office and partner agencies (2024), *National Zero-Emission Freight Corridor Strategy*.

title: Interoperable vehicle-to-grid operation
open: Can bidirectional (vehicle-to-grid) charging be made to work across arbitrary combinations of vehicles, chargers, aggregators, utilities, and regional grid codes, without requiring proprietary pairing between specific vendors? Formally, the goal is an engineering architecture and protocol stack achieving interoperable bidirectional charging across all such combinations.
status: The IEA’s 2026 assessment (IEA (2026), *Vehicle-to-grid technology*) describes commercial implementations alongside continuing interoperability and conformance work.
solved_when: A demonstrated system operates bidirectional charging across vehicle, charger, aggregator, utility, and regional grid-code combinations without proprietary pairing, meeting the relevant protocol conformance requirements.
why: A large theoretical storage resource is useless if only selected combinations of equipment and operators can participate in it.
key_works: IEA (2026), *Vehicle-to-grid technology*.

title: Battery-wear compensation for vehicle-to-grid
open: Can we estimate the incremental battery degradation caused by vehicle-to-grid use and translate it into fair compensation, warranty responsibility, and operating limits for each participant?
status: The IEA identifies battery-life and business-model questions as important deployment issues.
solved_when: A transparent mechanism exists that quantifies incremental degradation attributable to vehicle-to-grid operation and allocates compensation, warranty responsibility, and operating limits across participants in a verifiable way.
why: Grid-service revenue is not profit if vehicle owners absorb hidden battery costs; transparent allocation makes vehicle-to-grid participation economically honest.
key_works: IEA (2026), *Vehicle-to-grid technology*.

title: Firm grid services from uncertain vehicle availability
open: Can an aggregator of electric vehicles offer firm, dispatchable grid services despite the fact that individual vehicles may arrive late, depart early, change travel plans, or simply decline to participate? More formally, how should aggregate power commitments be computed and guaranteed under explicit models of mobility and participation uncertainty?
status: Aggregation of vehicles can provide grid services, but dependable commitments are not yet achieved; they require explicit modeling of mobility uncertainty and user guarantees. Key work: IEA (2026), *Vehicle-to-grid technology*.
solved_when: A method exists that provides reliable aggregate power commitments — i.e., commitments honored with high probability (or deterministic guarantees) under vehicle arrivals deviating in time, early departures, changed travel plans, and user opt-out — with explicit treatment of mobility uncertainty and user guarantees.
why: Transportation needs can override a grid dispatch instruction, so without explicit mobility-uncertainty modeling an aggregator's firm commitments may fail precisely when drivers' travel plans intervene.
key_works: IEA (2026), *Vehicle-to-grid technology*.

title: Charging reliability across weather and aging
open: How reliably do public EV fast-charging stations perform across real-world conditions — heat, cold, precipitation, equipment aging, and varying maintenance practices — and how can session failure rates be measurably reduced? Answering this requires longitudinal monitoring that tracks stations over seasons and equipment lifetimes rather than one-time audits.
status: Field audits have exposed charging failures, but full seasonal and lifecycle reliability remains a broader, unmet evidence requirement. Key work: Rempel et al. (2024), *Reliability of Open Public Electric Vehicle Direct Current Fast Chargers*.
solved_when: Session failure rates are quantified and reduced across heat, cold, precipitation, equipment age, and maintenance practices, using longitudinal evidence spanning seasons and equipment lifecycles rather than single audit snapshots.
why: A station that passes a one-time inspection may still fail for users year-round; longitudinal reliability data is what actually establishes dependable service.
key_works: Rempel et al. (2024), *Reliability of Open Public Electric Vehicle Direct Current Fast Chargers*.

title: Transport electrification with less critical-mineral dependence
open: Can transport electrification deliver the vehicle service society requires while materially reducing dependence on critical minerals? Formally, the goal is to combine battery chemistry, vehicle design, utilization, and recycling strategies so that required service is achieved with substantially lower critical-mineral demand.
status: The 2024 National Academies agenda (National Academies (2024), *Critical Issues in Transportation for 2024 and Beyond*, research appendix) identifies technical and cost barriers to less mineral-dependent battery designs.
solved_when: A demonstrated combination of battery chemistry, vehicle design, utilization, and recycling strategies achieves required vehicle service while materially reducing critical-mineral demand, overcoming the technical and cost barriers identified in the research agenda.
why: Decarbonization strategies that assume an unconstrained supply of critical minerals may fail when materials supply becomes a binding constraint; a solution decouples emissions reductions from mineral dependence.
key_works: National Academies (2024), *Critical Issues in Transportation for 2024 and Beyond*, research appendix.

title: Pavement lifecycle assessment with realistic use-phase feedback
open: Can pavement lifecycle assessment be made to capture how a road actually performs and is used over its whole life, rather than only what it costs to build? Concretely, this means integrating construction, maintenance, roughness-related vehicle energy, traffic delay, and end-of-life impacts within a single uncertainty-aware framework driven by local data.
status: Reference frameworks exist, notably Van Dam et al. (2015), *Towards Sustainable Pavement Systems: A Reference Document*, FHWA-HIF-15-002, but results remain sensitive to boundaries, deterioration assumptions, and traffic conditions.
solved_when: A lifecycle assessment framework exists that couples construction, maintenance, use-phase (roughness-induced vehicle energy and traffic delay), and end-of-life impacts, incorporates uncertainty using local data, and demonstrates that conclusions are robust to boundary choices, deterioration assumptions, and traffic conditions.
why: Low construction emissions do not necessarily imply low lifetime impact, so decisions based on upfront footprints alone can misdirect infrastructure investment.
key_works: Van Dam et al. (2015), *Towards Sustainable Pavement Systems: A Reference Document*, FHWA-HIF-15-002.

title: Recycled asphalt with predictable long-term durability
open: Can the long-term performance of recycled asphalt pavements be predicted reliably across the full range of reclaimed materials, rejuvenators, climates, and loading conditions — without relying solely on short-term laboratory proxies?
status: Recycling strategies for asphalt pavements are well established, but the reliable transfer of results from material tests to prediction of long service lives remains challenging. Key works: FHWA (2016), *Strategies for Improving the Sustainability of Asphalt Pavements*, FHWA-HIF-16-012.
solved_when: A validated framework exists that predicts long-term field performance of recycled asphalt across heterogeneous reclaimed materials, rejuvenators, climates, and loading, going beyond short-term laboratory material tests.
why: Premature pavement replacement can cancel out the material and emissions savings that recycling is meant to deliver.
key_works: FHWA (2016), *Strategies for Improving the Sustainability of Asphalt Pavements*, FHWA-HIF-16-012.

title: Pavement design for nonstationary climate
open: How should pavement design and rehabilitation decisions change when heat, rainfall, freeze–thaw, and flooding are treated as nonstationary climate processes rather than fixed historical statistics? A satisfactory answer translates projected climate trajectories into design choices with quantified failure probabilities.
status: Climate-adaptation guidance exists, notably FHWA (2015), *Climate Change Adaptation for Pavements* and FHWA pavement sustainability resources, but historical climate assumptions are insufficient for future service conditions.
solved_when: A design and rehabilitation framework is available that incorporates changing heat, rainfall, freeze–thaw, and flooding inputs and outputs quantified failure probabilities under future climate conditions.
why: Infrastructure may outlive the climate regime used to design it, so designs based on historical climate assumptions leave assets exposed to service conditions they were never designed for.
key_works: FHWA (2015), *Climate Change Adaptation for Pavements*; FHWA pavement sustainability resources.

title: Bridge condition to residual capacity
open: Can we infer a bridge's remaining load-bearing capacity and failure risk from inspection and sensing data, rather than treating visual condition ratings as direct measures of structural safety? Formally, the goal is a method that maps measured bridge condition evidence to quantitative estimates of residual capacity and failure probability.
status: The Long-Term Bridge Performance program collects richer evidence, and condition forecasting remains an active research product (FHWA, *Long-Term Bridge Performance Program* and *InfoBridge* condition-forecast research).
solved_when: A validated method exists that derives residual load-bearing capacity and failure risk from inspection and sensing data, demonstrated on data such as that collected by the Long-Term Bridge Performance program.
why: Similar visible damage can imply different structural consequences, so condition ratings alone misrank structural safety; a solution would let managers prioritize and intervene based on true risk rather than appearance.
key_works: FHWA, *Long-Term Bridge Performance Program* and *InfoBridge* condition-forecast research.

title: Tenfold cheaper decision-grade bridge inspection
open: Can the cost of obtaining a defensible bridge maintenance decision be cut tenfold — data collection, processing, and analysis together — without sacrificing detection sensitivity or well-calibrated uncertainty on the resulting recommendations?
status: Standardized inspection protocols and remote sensing provide the current foundations; however, cheaper data collection does not automatically translate into cheaper, reliable decision-making. Key reference: Hooks and Weidner, *Long-Term Bridge Performance Program Protocols, Version 1*, FHWA-HRT-16-007.
solved_when: A demonstrated inspection pipeline achieves at least a tenfold reduction in cost per defensible maintenance decision, while matching current detection sensitivity and maintaining calibrated uncertainty quantification.
why: It would make frequent, affordable assessment of large aging bridge inventories practical, so maintenance decisions rest on current evidence rather than sparse, aging inspections.
key_works: Hooks and Weidner, *Long-Term Bridge Performance Program Protocols, Version 1*, FHWA-HRT-16-007.

title: Abutment scour in cohesive soils
open: Can we predict how deeply flowing water will scour around a bridge abutment built in cohesive soils? The open goal is a validated prediction method for abutment scour in cohesive materials that holds across realistic hydraulic histories and geotechnical conditions.
status: A 2026 review (Sheefa, Liu, Vitton, and Barkdoll (2026), *A Review on Bridge Scour Analysis in Cohesive Soils and Scour-Susceptible Rocks*, DOI:10.3390/w18151879) finds that information on abutment scour remains comparatively limited relative to pier scour.
solved_when: A scour-prediction method for abutments in cohesive soils exists that is validated against experimental data covering realistic hydraulic histories and geotechnical conditions.
why: Current design extrapolates from sand-based formulas, which can misrepresent erosion in cohesive soils and leave abutments under- or over-designed.
key_works: Sheefa, Liu, Vitton, and Barkdoll (2026), *A Review on Bridge Scour Analysis in Cohesive Soils and Scour-Susceptible Rocks*, DOI:10.3390/w18151879.

title: Contraction scour in erodible rock
open: How deep will a bridge contraction scour into fractured or weathered rock — material that erodes neither like intact bedrock nor like cohesionless sediment? A predictive method is needed for contraction-driven erosion in such intermediate geomaterials.
status: The 2026 review by Sheefa et al. (2026), *A Review on Bridge Scour Analysis in Cohesive Soils and Scour-Susceptible Rocks*, identifies contraction scour in cohesive and rock formations as comparatively underdeveloped.
solved_when: A validated predictive model or experimental procedure exists for contraction scour depth in fractured or weathered rock, verified against physical experiments.
why: Without such a method, engineers may misclassify rock resistance and adopt unsafe foundation assumptions for bridge piers and abutments.
key_works: Sheefa et al. (2026), *A Review on Bridge Scour Analysis in Cohesive Soils and Scour-Susceptible Rocks*.

title: Undisturbed erodibility characterization
open: Can we obtain and test samples of cohesive soils and scour-susceptible rocks whose in-situ structure — the very fabric that governs erosion resistance — remains intact, and can we then measure how much the act of sampling itself biases the resulting erodibility estimates?
status: The 2026 scour review (Sheefa et al. (2026), *A Review on Bridge Scour Analysis in Cohesive Soils and Scour-Susceptible Rocks*) identifies undisturbed sampling and appropriate erodibility tests as critical unresolved practical needs.
solved_when: Undisturbed samples and an appropriate erodibility test protocol are obtained that preserve the in-situ structure controlling erosion, and the sampling-induced bias in measured erodibility is quantified.
why: Even a precise laboratory test can characterize the wrong material state, so scour predictions for cohesive soils and erodible rocks remain unreliable without knowing and correcting for sample disturbance.
key_works: Sheefa et al. (2026), *A Review on Bridge Scour Analysis in Cohesive Soils and Scour-Susceptible Rocks*.

title: Landscape-scale prediction of bridge scour
open: Can bridge scour be predicted at the scale of the surrounding landscape rather than just the bridge opening? That is, how can local scour calculations be coupled to channel migration, sediment supply, watershed change, and sequences of floods over a bridge’s service life?
status: Guidance and geomorphic research exist, but local hydraulic calculations do not capture every long-term landscape process. Key works: NCHRP (2011), *Evaluation of Bridge Scour Research: Geomorphic Processes and Predictions*, Web-Only Document 177; USGS (2003), *Guidance for Bridge Scour Studies*.
solved_when: A predictive framework exists that couples local scour calculations with long-term landscape processes — channel migration, sediment supply, watershed change, and service-life flood sequences — such that scour exposure at a bridge can be evaluated over its full service life.
why: A bridge foundation can become exposed through processes outside the immediate bridge opening, so purely local predictions miss the dominant long-term risks to the structure.
key_works: NCHRP (2011), *Evaluation of Bridge Scour Research: Geomorphic Processes and Predictions*, Web-Only Document 177; USGS (2003), *Guidance for Bridge Scour Studies*.

title: Causal service-life benefit of bridge maintenance
open: Estimate how specific maintenance interventions causally alter bridge deterioration and failure risk, correcting for the fact that the worst bridges receive treatment first. Formally, this calls for identifying intervention effects from observational maintenance histories with strong selection into treatment.
status: Longitudinal bridge programs provide data; observational maintenance histories contain strong selection effects. Key works: FHWA, *Long-Term Bridge Performance* program and InfoBridge research models.
solved_when: A method using longitudinal bridge-program data yields causal estimates of how specific interventions change deterioration rates and failure risk, valid under the selection effects present in observational maintenance histories.
why: Better deterioration forecasts do not automatically identify better interventions; without causal estimates, maintenance decisions may target the wrong treatments.
key_works: FHWA, *Long-Term Bridge Performance* program and InfoBridge research models.

title: Comparable non-exhaust particulate inventories
open: Can we build comparable inventories of non-exhaust traffic particulates — tire, brake, road-wear, and resuspended particles — that reconcile across vehicle classes, operating conditions, and measurement methods? Formally, this asks for a standardized attribution framework under which different measurement approaches yield consistent, comparable emission estimates.
status: Non-exhaust emissions are recognized as important, but standardized attribution and comparable inventories remain difficult, as documented in OECD (2020), *Non-exhaust Particulate Emissions from Road Transport: An Ignored Environmental Policy Challenge*, DOI:10.1787/4a4dc6ca-en.
solved_when: A standardized methodology exists that measures and reconciles tire, brake, road-wear, and resuspended particle emissions across vehicle classes, operating conditions, and measurement methods, yielding comparable inventories.
why: Electrification does not remove all traffic-related particulate pollution, so non-exhaust sources will dominate remaining traffic emissions without a way to attribute and compare them.
key_works: OECD (2020), *Non-exhaust Particulate Emissions from Road Transport: An Ignored Environmental Policy Challenge*, DOI:10.1787/4a4dc6ca-en.

title: Regenerative braking’s real particle effects
open: How much does regenerative braking actually reduce brake particle emissions over a real duty cycle, and how do the emitted particles themselves change in character across regenerative strategies, friction-brake use, corrosion, and emergency braking? A rigorous answer requires quantifying both particle reductions and shifts in particle characteristics under each braking regime.
status: It is known that regeneration changes brake use, but whole-duty-cycle emissions depend on more than total braking energy; no quantified reductions or particle-characterization results are recorded. Key works: Costagliola et al. (2024), *Non-Exhaust Particulate Particulate Emissions from Road Transport Vehicles*, DOI:10.3390/en17164079.
solved_when: An experimental characterization delivers quantified brake-particle reductions and changed particle characteristics across regenerative strategies, friction-brake use, corrosion, and emergency braking, sufficient to replace fixed assumed reduction factors in fleet models.
why: Fleet-scale emission models currently rely on fixed assumed reduction factors; realistic, duty-cycle-dependent measurements would make their benefit estimates credible.
key_works: Costagliola et al. (2024), *Non-Exhaust Particulate Emissions from Road Transport Vehicles*, DOI:10.3390/en17164079.

title: Safer replacements for 6PPD
open: Can we find tire-protection chemistries that preserve the safety and durability that 6PPD provides, without producing transformation products of comparable environmental harm? Formally, the goal is to identify and validate functional replacements for 6PPD whose environmental transformation products are substantially less toxic.
status: Acute toxicity of 6PPD-quinone to coho salmon is established (Tian et al. (2021), *A ubiquitous tire rubber-derived chemical induces acute mortality in coho salmon*, DOI:10.1126/science.abd6951); finding and validating safer functional replacements is a distinct, still-open problem.
solved_when: A replacement chemistry is identified and experimentally validated to maintain tire protection performance while avoiding transformation products with toxicity comparable to 6PPD-quinone.
why: Removing an environmental hazard must not come at the cost of tire integrity, so any viable substitution must satisfy both performance and toxicological criteria.
key_works: Tian et al. (2021), *A ubiquitous tire rubber-derived chemical induces acute mortality in coho salmon*, DOI:10.1126/science.abd6951.

title: Fate and chronic effects of tire-derived toxicants
open: How do tire-derived toxicants move through and transform in the environment, and what chronic effects do they cause across watersheds and species beyond the initially identified acute endpoint? More precisely, we need to determine the transport, transformation, bioavailability, and chronic toxicity of these chemicals across ecosystems.
status: Identification of one potent toxicant (Tian et al. (2021), *A ubiquitous tire rubber-derived chemical induces acute mortality in coho salmon*) does not complete environmental fate or ecosystem-risk assessment.
solved_when: The transport, transformation, bioavailability, and chronic effects of tire-derived toxicants have been experimentally characterized across watersheds and species beyond the initially identified acute mortality endpoint in coho salmon.
why: A solution directly guides runoff treatment design and material substitution decisions toward the exposure pathways that actually matter.
key_works: Tian et al. (2021), *A ubiquitous tire rubber-derived chemical induces acute mortality in coho salmon*.

title: Low-wear tires without safety or energy penalties
open: Can tire wear particles be reduced without sacrificing the safety, efficiency, or longevity that current tires deliver? Formally, the challenge is to advance the joint frontier of particle generation, wet grip, rolling resistance, durability, and cold-weather performance.
status: Non-exhaust mitigation is an active policy and engineering need; optimizing one property can degrade another. Key works: OECD (2020), *Non-exhaust Particulate Emissions from Road Transport*; Costagliola et al. (2024), *Non-Exhaust Particulate Emissions from Road Transport Vehicles*.
solved_when: A tire design (or material/compound) is demonstrated, experimentally, to reduce particle generation while matching or improving current levels of wet grip, rolling resistance, durability, and cold-weather performance.
why: It prevents emissions improvements that backfire by increasing crashes or energy consumption, addressing a mitigation need that currently cannot be met by optimizing any single property alone.
key_works: OECD (2020), *Non-exhaust Particulate Emissions from Road Transport*; Costagliola et al. (2024), *Non-Exhaust Particulate Emissions from Road Transport Vehicles*.

title: Probabilistic transport design under climate uncertainty
open: How can transport infrastructure design standards explicitly account for hazard distributions that shift over time, for disagreement among climate models, and for the real consequences of failure? The goal is a framework that turns deep uncertainty into probabilistic design requirements rather than a single fixed scenario.
status: Resilience guidance is advancing, but translating uncertainty into procurement-ready design requirements remains difficult. Key work: Global Center on Adaptation (2025), *Climate-Resilient Infrastructure Officer Handbook*.
solved_when: A usable design standard exists that incorporates changing hazard distributions, model disagreement, and failure consequences in a form ready for procurement and engineering practice.
why: Neither historical return periods nor any single climate scenario is sufficient for design under a changing climate; without such standards, resilience guidance cannot be translated into actual procurement decisions.
key_works: Global Center on Adaptation (2025), *Climate-Resilient Infrastructure Officer Handbook*.

title: Cascading transport–power–water failures
open: Can coupled transport–power–water systems be modeled so that a cascade in which transport disruption blocks utility repair while utility outages disable transport operations is predicted — and then reduced? Formally, the goal is a tractable coupled model that captures this mutual-disablement feedback and identifies interventions that cut it off.
status: Infrastructure resilience research recognizes interdependence, but actionable coupled models remain demanding. Key works: Hallegatte, Rentschler, and Rozenberg (2019), *Lifelines: The Resilient Infrastructure Opportunity*; GFDRR resilient-infrastructure program.
solved_when: A coupled model exists that predicts such cascades and demonstrates a measurable reduction of them; no quantitative targets (round counts, exponents, budgets, sizes) are stated in the record, so the natural engineering criterion is predictive accuracy on the coupled cascade plus a validated intervention that reduces it relative to independent (uncoupled) baselines.
why: Hardening each infrastructure system independently can miss shared failure pathways, so interventions designed in silo may leave the dominant cascade route untouched.
key_works: Hallegatte, Rentschler, and Rozenberg (2019), *Lifelines: The Resilient Infrastructure Opportunity*; GFDRR resilient-infrastructure program.

title: Equitable restoration of transportation access
open: When a disrupted transportation network must be restored under limited resources, can repair and temporary service be prioritized by essential-access loss and community vulnerability rather than by traffic volume or economic output alone?
status: Resilience frameworks such as Hallegatte, Rentschler, and Rozenberg (2019), *Lifelines*, and GFDRR, *Resilient Infrastructure*, emphasize service consequences, but operational equity criteria remain difficult to specify and validate.
solved_when: A theory exists that specifies operational equity criteria — based on essential-access loss and vulnerability — for prioritizing repairs and temporary service, together with a way to validate them on disrupted networks.
why: Low-volume links can be indispensable to isolated communities, so volume- or output-based prioritization can leave essential access unrestored indefinitely.
key_works: Hallegatte, Rentschler, and Rozenberg (2019), *Lifelines*; GFDRR, *Resilient Infrastructure*.

title: Avoiding transport adaptation that relocates risk
open: Does transport adaptation — raising, defending, rerouting, or expanding infrastructure — simply relocate flood risk rather than reduce it, increasing exposure, displacement, or ecological damage elsewhere?
status: Climate-resilience guidance increasingly requires systemwide assessment; local asset protection is not sufficient evidence of net benefit. Key work: Global Center on Adaptation (2025), *Climate-Resilient Infrastructure Officer Handbook*.
solved_when: A method exists to evaluate whether a given adaptation measure changes flood exposure, displacement, or ecological damage systemwide; success means showing net benefit (or harm) beyond the protected asset itself.
why: A protected road can worsen flooding or access for neighboring communities, so local asset protection alone is not evidence of a good outcome.
key_works: Global Center on Adaptation (2025), *Climate-Resilient Infrastructure Officer Handbook*.

title: Operational adaptation to compound extremes
open: Can essential mobility be maintained when a transportation system is hit by compound extremes — heat plus power outage, wildfire plus evacuation, or flooding plus communications failure? More formally, the question is how to design operational adaptation so that mobility remains functional under such concurrent hazard combinations, rather than under each hazard in isolation.
status: Transportation resilience conferences document these challenges, but compound-event operations remain more complex than existing single-hazard plans. Key work: National Academies (2025), *Transportation Resilience 2023: International Conference on Extreme Weather and Climate Change Challenges*, DOI:10.17226/28858.
solved_when: An operational approach (plan, protocol, or experimentally validated strategy) demonstrates that essential mobility is maintained during compound-event combinations such as heat plus power outage, wildfire plus evacuation, or flooding plus communications failure — not merely during single-hazard scenarios.
why: Contingency plans that are each adequate on their own can fail when activated together, so without explicit treatment of compound extremes, supposedly resilient systems may collapse precisely when multiple stresses strike at once.
key_works: National Academies (2025), *Transportation Resilience 2023: International Conference on Extreme Weather and Climate Change Challenges*, DOI:10.17226/28858.

title: Replacing fuel taxes without regressive surveillance
subfield: Institutions, financing, rural access, and informal transport
open: How can governments replace fuel taxes with road-revenue systems that do not require surveillance of where and when people drive, remain affordable across income groups, and stay administratively practical as vehicles shift away from gasoline and diesel?
status: The National Academies identify replacement revenue and equity consequences as unresolved policy questions (National Academies (2024), *Critical Issues in Transportation for 2024 and Beyond*, "Funding and Finance").
solved_when: A durable road-revenue mechanism is demonstrated that protects privacy, addresses affordability, and remains administratively workable despite changing vehicle energy sources.
why: Infrastructure funding cannot depend indefinitely on declining taxable fuel consumption; as vehicles electrify, the tax base erodes and an inequitable or privacy-invading replacement becomes the default outcome.
key_works: National Academies (2024), *Critical Issues in Transportation for 2024 and Beyond*, “Funding and Finance.”

title: Binding maintenance funding commitments
subfield: Institutions, financing, rural access, and informal transport
open: How can funding and accountability arrangements be designed so that predictable maintenance needs are not repeatedly deferred in favor of more visible projects?
status: Maintenance and financial sustainability remain recurring transport funding problems, as highlighted in National Academies (2024), *Critical Issues in Transportation for 2024 and Beyond*, "Funding and Finance."
solved_when: A funding and accountability mechanism is specified that demonstrably prevents recurring deferral of maintenance in favor of more visible projects.
why: Deferred work can turn manageable deterioration into costly loss of service.
key_works: National Academies (2024), *Critical Issues in Transportation for 2024 and Beyond*, “Funding and Finance.”

title: Cross-jurisdiction corridor coordination
subfield: Institutions, financing, rural access, and informal transport
open: How should investment, operating responsibility, and benefits be allocated across jurisdictions whose local incentives conflict with corridor-wide performance? A satisfactory answer is an allocation mechanism under which corridor-wide performance is achieved despite each jurisdiction acting on its own incentives.
status: Fragmented governance is an identified barrier, and it is recognized that cooperation requires more than compatible engineering designs; see National Academies (2024), *Critical Issues in Transportation for 2024 and Beyond*, "Governance."
solved_when: A criterion (theoretical mechanism or funding/institutional arrangement) is specified that allocates investment, operating responsibility, and benefits across jurisdictions and is shown to reconcile local incentives with corridor-wide performance.
why: Bottlenecks and externalities routinely cross administrative boundaries, so outcomes hinge on governance structures rather than engineering compatibility alone.
key_works: National Academies (2024), *Critical Issues in Transportation for 2024 and Beyond*, “Governance.”

title: When private provision actually improves outcomes
subfield: Institutions, financing, rural access, and informal transport
open: Under what causal conditions does private participation in transport provision actually improve lifecycle cost, service quality, innovation, and risk allocation, rather than merely changing the accounting treatment of the same outcomes?
status: Comparative governance remains context-dependent; ownership labels alone do not predict performance. Key work: National Academies (2024), *Critical Issues in Transportation for 2024 and Beyond*, "Governance."
solved_when: A set of causal conditions is identified under which private participation demonstrably improves lifecycle cost, service, innovation, and risk allocation — beyond accounting effects.
why: Poorly allocated risk can leave the public paying for nominally private projects, so knowing these conditions determines when privatization delivers real gains versus shifted liabilities.
key_works: National Academies (2024), *Critical Issues in Transportation for 2024 and Beyond*, “Governance.”

title: Retaining public-sector transport expertise
subfield: Institutions, financing, rural access, and informal transport
open: How can public transport agencies build staffing, procurement, compensation, training, and career structures that retain the technical capacity needed to oversee increasingly complex systems?
status: The 2024 workforce agenda explicitly identifies attraction, training, and retention as unresolved needs. Key work: National Academies (2024), *Critical Issues in Transportation for 2024 and Beyond*, "Workforce."
solved_when: An experimental or funded intervention demonstrates that specific staffing, procurement, compensation, training, or career-structure reforms measurably improve retention of technical capacity in agencies overseeing complex transport systems.
why: Agencies cannot effectively buy or regulate systems they cannot evaluate; retaining technical expertise is the precondition for competent oversight.
key_works: National Academies (2024), *Critical Issues in Transportation for 2024 and Beyond*, “Workforce.”

title: Complementary investments that make rural roads productive
subfield: Institutions, financing, rural access, and informal transport
open: Which complementary investments turn a rural road into a sustained increase in household living standards? Formally, what combinations of transport services, finance, skills, and market institutions, layered onto improved connectivity, generate lasting income gains rather than mere labor reallocation?
status: Existing rural-road evidence — notably Asher and Novosad (2020), *Rural Roads and Local Economic Development*, DOI:10.1257/aer.20180268 — shows labor reallocation without automatic broad income gains over the measured horizon.
solved_when: A study (or set of studies) identifies specific combinations of roads, services, finance, skills, and market institutions, with credible experimental or quasi-experimental evidence, that convert improved connectivity into sustained broad household income gains over the measured horizon.
why: Connectivity is an input to development, not a guarantee of it; without knowing which complements matter, road spending risks producing reallocated labor without broad-based gains.
key_works: Asher and Novosad (2020), *Rural Roads and Local Economic Development*, DOI:10.1257/aer.20180268.

title: Rural access beyond proximity to a road
subfield: Institutions, financing, rural access, and informal transport
open: Can we measure whether rural people can actually afford and obtain reliable transport to essential destinations, rather than merely whether an all-season road is nearby?
status: Rural Access Index methods improve physical-connectivity measurement; service availability and affordability require additional indicators. Key work: World Bank (2016), *Measuring Rural Access: Using New Technologies*.
solved_when: A measurement method exists that captures service availability and affordability — not just physical connectivity — using indicators beyond road proximity.
why: A nearby road without usable transport does not provide effective access, so current proximity-based measures overstate real access.
key_works: World Bank (2016), *Measuring Rural Access: Using New Technologies*.

title: Dynamic seasonal passability maps
subfield: Institutions, financing, rural access, and informal transport
open: Can we build route-level passability maps that stay current through rain, flooding, erosion, and seasonal closures, so that fixed road inventories stop misleading planners? Formally, the goal is to maintain dynamically updated accessibility information at route level as conditions change seasonally and after weather events.
status: Geospatial rural-access methods exist, as reflected in the World Bank (2019), *Measuring Rural Access: Update 2017/18*, and the Rural Access Index data program, but continually updated operational accessibility remains a larger data challenge.
solved_when: An operational system continually updates route-level passability information through rain, flooding, erosion, and seasonal closures, beyond the fixed road inventories that currently mislead.
why: Annual average access figures can conceal months of isolation, so dynamic maps would reveal the true seasonal deprivation rural populations face.
key_works: World Bank (2019), *Measuring Rural Access: Update 2017/18*; Rural Access Index data program.

title: Maintained maps of informal transit
subfield: Institutions, financing, rural access, and informal transport
open: How can maps of informal transit — routes, stops, fares, operating periods, and service changes — be kept continuously current in systems that have no formal schedules or centralized operator records?
status: Digital Matatus demonstrated practical mapping and standardized data; long-term maintenance and scaling remain distinct challenges. Key works: Digital Matatus project; MIT Department of Urban Studies and Planning, *Digital Matatus*.
solved_when: A working approach exists that keeps route, stop, fare, and service-change data accurate over time without relying on formal schedules or centralized operator records, and that demonstrably scales beyond an initial mapping effort.
why: One-time maps quickly lose value in adaptive transport systems, so maintenance capability is what determines whether mapping investments pay off.
key_works: Digital Matatus project; MIT Department of Urban Studies and Planning, *Digital Matatus*.

title: Routing through unscheduled informal services
subfield: Institutions, financing, rural access, and informal transport
open: Can we build journey planners that give useful multimodal predictions in transport systems where departures, routes, fares, and transfer opportunities are uncertain or negotiated rather than fixed? In formal terms, this asks for routing under uncertainty models that go beyond static route geometry and partially observed service availability.
status: Mapping informal networks has been shown feasible, notably through the Digital Matatus research and data program, but dependable journey planning still requires uncertainty models beyond static route geometry.
solved_when: A journey-planning method exists that produces dependable multimodal predictions for informal services despite uncertain departures, routes, fares, and transfer opportunities.
why: Treating informal transit as either perfectly scheduled or nonexistent both misrepresent mobility, so current planners fail exactly where much of the world's transport is informal.
key_works: Digital Matatus research and data program.

title: Useful mobility data without reidentification
subfield: Transportation data, cybersecurity, and benchmark infrastructure
open: Can detailed human mobility data be released or analyzed while provably bounding the risk of reidentification when adversaries hold realistic auxiliary information? Formally, the challenge is to quantify — and then limit — identification risk under assumptions about what an attacker already knows.
status: Mobility traces have long been shown to be highly identifying, and removing names is not adequate protection; the key evidence is de Montjoye, Hidalgo, Verleysen, and Blondel (2013), *Unique in the Crowd: The privacy bounds of human mobility*, DOI:10.1038/srep01376. Related lines of work include differential privacy and linkage attacks.
solved_when: A release mechanism or analysis framework exists that preserves useful movement detail while providing a demonstrable bound on reidentification risk under realistic auxiliary information.
why: Transportation research depends on movement data whose very detail makes it inherently sensitive, so without such guarantees either privacy is violated or the data is withheld or degraded beyond usefulness.
key_works: de Montjoye, Hidalgo, Verleysen, and Blondel (2013), *Unique in the Crowd: The privacy bounds of human mobility*, DOI:10.1038/srep01376.

title: Privacy for rare origin–destination movements
subfield: Transportation data, cybersecurity, and benchmark infrastructure
open: Can we release origin–destination mobility statistics that remain useful for rare trips and underserved populations while still providing meaningful privacy protection across repeated releases?
status: High mobility uniqueness makes the utility–privacy trade-off especially difficult for sparse movements, as shown by de Montjoye et al. (2013), *Unique in the Crowd*, DOI:10.1038/srep01376.
solved_when: A mechanism is given that, over repeated data releases, simultaneously preserves accurate estimates for rare origin–destination movements and underserved groups and provides formal privacy protection; the record states no further quantitative targets.
why: Privacy mechanisms that suppress rare travel patterns can erase from the data exactly the people most in need of transportation service, so getting this trade-off right determines whether privacy and equity can coexist.
key_works: de Montjoye et al. (2013), *Unique in the Crowd*, DOI:10.1038/srep01376.

title: Safe vehicles connected to compromised chargers
subfield: Transportation data, cybersecurity, and benchmark infrastructure
open: Can a vehicle remain safe when plugged into a charger an adversary controls? Formally, design and validate vehicle-side mechanisms that prevent a malicious or compromised charger from inducing unsafe vehicle behavior or propagating access into safety-critical systems.
status: NHTSA identifies compromised charging infrastructure and zero-trust vehicle architectures as active research concerns (NHTSA (2024), *NHTSA/SAE Cybersecurity Workshop Keynote* and associated research agenda).
solved_when: An engineering design (with validation or benchmark evidence) exists showing that a compromised charger cannot induce unsafe vehicle behavior or propagate access into safety-critical vehicle systems.
why: Charging expands the boundary between vehicles and externally controlled systems, so charger compromise is a direct pathway to safety-critical vehicle functions.
key_works: NHTSA (2024), *NHTSA/SAE Cybersecurity Workshop Keynote* and associated research agenda.

title: Safe over-the-air update and rollback
subfield: Transportation data, cybersecurity, and benchmark infrastructure
open: Can we guarantee that an interrupted, inconsistent, or rolled-back over-the-air update never leaves a vehicle in an unsafe combination of software and calibration? Formally, this asks for a verification framework establishing compositional correctness of the vehicle configuration across all possible update and rollback sequences.
status: NHTSA's 2022 practices address cybersecurity and software assurance for modern vehicles (NHTSA (2022), *Cybersecurity Best Practices for the Safety of Modern Vehicles*), but fleet-wide compositional correctness remains an engineering target.
solved_when: A method exists that verifies, for every possible interruption, inconsistency, or rollback scenario, that the resulting combination of vehicle software and calibration is safe — with compositional correctness holding fleet-wide.
why: Individually valid components can combine into an invalid, unsafe vehicle configuration, so per-component assurance alone does not protect the vehicle.
key_works: NHTSA (2022), *Cybersecurity Best Practices for the Safety of Modern Vehicles*.

title: Detecting correlated fleet cyber failures
subfield: Transportation data, cybersecurity, and benchmark infrastructure
open: Can we reliably tell the difference between a coordinated cyber attack on a fleet and the ordinary confusion of shared software bugs, weather effects, or normal operating variability — early enough that response can contain the harm?
status: NHTSA (2024), *NHTSA/SAE Cybersecurity Workshop Keynote*, emphasizes expanded attack surfaces and industrywide information sharing; reliable detection and response remain ongoing needs.
solved_when: A detection method exists that distinguishes coordinated cyber compromise from common-cause defects, weather effects, and normal fleet behavior, with early enough warning to contain harm.
why: A single shared dependency can turn one weakness into simultaneous failures across the fleet, so without such detection one compromise cascades before it is recognized.
key_works: NHTSA (2024), *NHTSA/SAE Cybersecurity Workshop Keynote*.

title: Comparable cross-modal funding and performance data
subfield: Transportation data, cybersecurity, and benchmark infrastructure
open: Can the United States build and maintain a single, comparable data record that links revenues, subsidies, asset condition, service output, and outcomes across roads, transit, ports, and airports? Formally, the goal is a maintained cross-modal dataset whose accounting conventions allow like-for-like comparison of funding and performance.
status: The 2024 National Academies appendix identifies major gaps in aggregated cross-modal financial and performance metrics; no such comparable cross-modal record currently exists. Key work: National Academies (2024), *Critical Issues in Transportation for 2024 and Beyond*, research and metrics appendix.
solved_when: A maintained, publicly available dataset exists that links revenues, subsidies, asset condition, service output, and outcomes for roads, transit, ports, and airports on comparable accounting conventions, covering the gaps the 2024 National Academies appendix identifies.
why: Incompatible accounting currently obstructs rational comparisons across modes and undermines accountability for how transportation money translates into condition and outcomes.
key_works: National Academies (2024), *Critical Issues in Transportation for 2024 and Beyond*, research and metrics appendix.

title: Confidential freight data sharing
subfield: Transportation data, cybersecurity, and benchmark infrastructure
open: Can carriers, shippers, and logistics hubs jointly optimize freight operations and verify each other's performance without revealing competitively sensitive information such as customer identities, prices, capacities, or operating practices? In formal terms, the goal is a construction in which collaborative optimization and verification are carried out under privacy constraints on all inputs.
status: Shared logistics architectures need information exchange, but commercial confidentiality remains a participation barrier. The Physical Internet vision is articulated in Montreuil (2011), *Toward a Physical Internet*, DOI:10.1007/s12159-011-0045-x. Related lines of work include secure multiparty computation and privacy-preserving optimization.
solved_when: A working confidential freight data-sharing architecture exists in which joint optimization and performance verification succeed without exposing customers, prices, capacities, or operating practices.
why: Freight collaboration requires more than asking firms to publish their data; without confidentiality guarantees, commercial sensitivity remains a barrier to participation in shared logistics architectures.
key_works: Montreuil (2011), *Toward a Physical Internet*, DOI:10.1007/s12159-011-0045-x.

title: Prioritizing cyber defenses by physical consequence
subfield: Transportation data, cybersecurity, and benchmark infrastructure
open: Can cyber vulnerabilities in transportation systems be ranked by the credible physical safety consequences they enable — including interacting failures — rather than by software severity alone? A formalization would score each vulnerability or mitigation according to the severity and likelihood of the physical harm that results, accounting for how failures interact.
status: NHTSA's research agenda explicitly raises criticality and standardized threat-analysis questions, as noted in NHTSA (2024), *NHTSA/SAE Cybersecurity Workshop Keynote*.
solved_when: A method exists for ranking vulnerabilities and mitigations by credible physical safety consequences, including interacting failures, that is usable in practice rather than relying on software severity alone.
why: The most visible software weakness may not create the greatest physical risk, so defenses prioritized by software severity alone can misallocate protection away from the faults that actually endanger people.
key_works: NHTSA (2024), *NHTSA/SAE Cybersecurity Workshop Keynote*.

title: Representative disability mobility data with privacy
subfield: Transportation data, cybersecurity, and benchmark infrastructure
open: How can we collect longitudinal mobility data detailed enough to reveal disability-specific travel barriers, without exposing individuals' health status, daily routines, or sensitive destinations?
status: National surveys provide important population evidence; fine-grained longitudinal evaluation creates additional privacy and sampling challenges. Key works: BTS, *Travel Patterns of American Adults with Disabilities*; de Montjoye et al. (2013), *Unique in the Crowd*.
solved_when: A data collection and protection methodology exists that supports fine-grained longitudinal, disability-stratified evaluation of travel barriers while safeguarding participants' health status, routines, and sensitive destinations; success is measured by both adequate representation of small disability populations and demonstrable privacy protection.
why: Small populations need both stronger representation and stronger protection; without such data, disability-specific transportation barriers cannot be evaluated at fine temporal grain.
key_works: BTS, *Travel Patterns of American Adults with Disabilities*; de Montjoye et al. (2013), *Unique in the Crowd*.

title: Fresh and contamination-resistant driving benchmarks
subfield: Transportation data, cybersecurity, and benchmark infrastructure
open: How can we maintain driving-policy evaluation sets that stay trustworthy as evidence over time — detecting training leakage, repeated test-set optimization, scenario aging, and geographic overfitting? In formal terms, what benchmark-refresh and contamination-audit procedures preserve independence between training and evaluation as models and datasets co-evolve?
status: Large closed-loop benchmarks exist, such as Caesar et al. (2021), *nuPlan*, arXiv:2106.11810, and Gulino et al. (2023), *Waymax*, arXiv:2310.08710, but fixed public benchmarks do not automatically remain independent evidence as models and datasets evolve.
solved_when: A benchmark maintenance methodology exists that demonstrably detects training leakage, repeated test-set optimization, scenario aging, and geographic overfitting in driving-policy evaluation.
why: Without such maintenance, measured benchmark progress can reflect familiarity with the test set rather than genuinely safer driving.
key_works: Caesar et al. (2021), *nuPlan*, arXiv:2106.11810; Gulino et al. (2023), *Waymax*, arXiv:2310.08710.

title: Repurposed hydrogen-pipeline integrity
open: Can we predict, with quantified confidence, the safe operating envelope of an existing natural-gas pipeline repurposed for hydrogen service? Formally, this requires a predictive integrity framework covering welds, defects, fatigue crack growth under pressure cycling, and uncertain material histories.
