status: Repurposing assessments have identified important material and risk-model gaps, and it is known that suitability cannot be inferred from original gas service alone; see Yang et al. (2024), *Research gaps in quantitative risk assessment of hydrogen transmission pipelines*; Future Fuels CRC, *Review of future fuels transport and storage technologies*.
solved_when: A validated method exists for determining safe operating envelopes (pressure, cycling regime, defect acceptance limits) for existing pipelines exposed to hydrogen, explicitly accounting for welds, defects, fatigue, pressure cycling, and uncertain material histories.
why: Demonstrated integrity is the gate on reuse: repurposing existing pipelines could avoid major new infrastructure construction, but only where safety can be established.
key_works: Yang et al. (2024), *Research gaps in quantitative risk assessment of hydrogen transmission pipelines*; Future Fuels CRC, *Review of future fuels transport and storage technologies*.

title: Empirical failure frequencies for hydrogen pipelines
open: Can we build incident-frequency and consequence models for hydrogen pipelines — both new builds and repurposed networks — that are statistically defensible despite sparse operating experience?
status: Quantitative risk assessments remain constrained by limited hydrogen-specific incident and failure data; Yang et al. (2024), *Research gaps in quantitative risk assessment of hydrogen transmission pipelines*, document these gaps.
solved_when: Quantitative risk assessments for hydrogen transmission pipelines rest on empirically grounded failure-frequency estimates with explicit uncertainty quantification, rather than poorly supported event frequencies.
why: Precise-looking risk calculations can conceal poorly supported event frequencies, undermining decisions on hydrogen network safety and deployment.
key_works: Yang et al. (2024), *Research gaps in quantitative risk assessment of hydrogen transmission pipelines*.

title: Repeatable microgravity cryogenic transfer
open: Can repeated cryogenic propellant transfer be demonstrated reliably under microgravity conditions, with vapor ingestion, chilldown loss, pressure behavior, gauging, and coupling all kept under control throughout?
status: Mission studies and component development provide the current foundations, but integrated repeatable transfer remains a distinct, undemonstrated operational requirement. See Meyer et al. (2021), *Recent Concept Study for Cryogenic Fluid Management to Support Opposition Class Crewed Missions to Mars*, NASA NTRS 20210024129.
solved_when: An integrated, repeatable transfer demonstration under relevant microgravity conditions shows controlled vapor ingestion, chilldown loss, pressure, gauging, and coupling behavior across repeated operations.
why: It is the enabling capability for reusable in-space transport and orbital propellant depots.
key_works: Meyer et al. (2021), *Recent Concept Study for Cryogenic Fluid Management to Support Opposition Class Crewed Missions to Mars*, NASA NTRS 20210024129.

title: Long-duration low-loss cryogenic transport
open: Can a cryogenic propellant system keep its cargo usable throughout a long mission, despite continuous heat leaks, intermittent active cooling, power interruptions, slosh, and rising tank pressure? Formally stated as an engineering goal: demonstrate an integrated long-duration storage and transport system that preserves usable cryogenic propellant under these coupled effects.
status: Technology roadmaps identify the coupled storage and transfer needs, but component maturity alone does not establish complete mission reliability. Key works: Stephens (2017), *Cryogenic Fluid Management Technology Development Roadmaps*, NASA NTRS 20170004449; Meyer et al. (2021), NTRS 20210024129.
solved_when: An integrated cryogenic storage and transfer system demonstrates complete mission reliability under combined heat leaks, active cooling with power interruptions, slosh, and tank pressure — not merely component-level maturity.
why: Propellant lost while waiting can dominate the mass budget of space logistics, so low-loss storage directly determines how much useful mission payload survives.
key_works: Stephens (2017), *Cryogenic Fluid Management Technology Development Roadmaps*, NASA NTRS 20170004449; Meyer et al. (2021), NTRS 20210024129.
